questions.question:
A 34-year-old woman is admitted via the Emergency Department after suffering acute lower back pain. X-ray in the department revealed two compression fractures suspicious of osteoporosis. Past medical history of note includes depression and anxiety. On examination, her body mass index (BMI) is 16 kg/m² and her blood pressure is 125/72 mmHg, with a pulse of 55/min and regular.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)112 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)4.6 × 10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)202 × 10⁹/L150 - 400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)102 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Corrected calcium (Ca²⁺)2.2 mmol/L2.2 - 2.7 mmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)115 U/L30 - 150 U/L
T-score–3.1

Which of the following is likely to be the most important contributory factor to her condition?
options: Low BMI leading to secondary ovarian failure
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Low BMI leading to secondary ovarian failure

This patient has a very low BMI (and is slightly bradycardic), and further questioning may reveal that she is not currently menstruating and may not have been for some time. This leads to a lack of oestrogenisation and consequent negative effects on bone mineral density. Increased BMI in contrast is associated with increased bone mineral density up to the point of development of type 2 diabetes, when a fall in BMD and increased risk of fracture is seen.

B Genetic predisposition to osteoporosis

Clearly a genetic predisposition to osteoporosis might also increase the risk of fracture at an early age, but BMI is almost certainly the greatest contributor to risk here.

C Hyperthyroidism

Hyperthyroidism is another possibility, but we are given no information that she has symptoms or signs of this and indeed she is bradycardic, not tachycardic.

D Hypovitaminosis D

Although a risk factor for demineralisation of bone, her biggest risk factor is low BMI.

E Calcium deficiency

Her calcium is in the normal range.

questions.question: A 34-year-old, right-handed woman complains of pain in her right wrist which has been evident for 3 months. Recently she has also noted some pain in her left wrist, although of much less severity. She works at a till in a superstore and has been finding it difficult to continue with her job. The examination reveals a localised swelling and tenderness over the lateral, dorsal aspect of the right wrist and mild tenderness in the left wrist, particularly over the radial aspect. The haematology and biochemistry blood test results are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A De Quervain’s tenosynovitis

This lady has tenderness at the thumb-sided tendons – at the radial side of the wrist and at the base of the thumb – and probably has an occupational aetiology given her job as checkout cashier. De Quervain’s tenosynovitis refers to inflammation of the abductor pollicis longus tendon at the wrist joint. It is best diagnosed by inspecting the wrist from the radial side, with the palms together. It is then seen as a unilateral swelling, extending from the first carpometacarpal joint proximally. The diagnosis is confirmed by Finkelstein’s test. In this test, the patient is asked to bring the thumb across the palm and clasp the fingers around it. The examiner then pulls it in the ulnar direction, which elicits a sharp pain. This condition is commonly caused by occupational or avocational repetitive movement of the thumb, but has also been associated with RA, psoriatic arthritis, direct trauma, pregnancy and the post-partum period. Treatment options include splinting, steroid injections into the joint and surgical decompression of the tendon tunnel.

B Intersection syndrome

This lady has irritation at the first dorsal compartment. Intersection syndrome is a painful condition that affects the thumb side of the forearm when inflammation occurs at the intersection of the muscle bellies of the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis crossing over the extensor carpi radialis longus and the extensor carpi radialis brevis. These 1st and 2nd dorsal muscle compartments intersect at this location, hence the name. The mechanism of injury is usually repetitive resisted extension, as with rowing, weight-lifting or pulling.

C Wrist synovitis

This lady has localised swelling at the radial side (not the whole wrist). Wrist synovitis is inflammation of the wrist joint and therefore the whole wrist would be swollen diffusely.

D Ganglion

A ganglion is a discrete, palpable lump.

E Trigger thumb

A trigger digit is a common disorder characterised by catching, snapping or locking of the involved finger flexor tendon, associated with dysfunction and pain.

questions.question: A 34-year old woman is due to be discharged after being admitted for iloprost infusion for systemic sclerosis. She was admitted due to poorly controlled digital ulceration. A photograph of her hands is shown below. This is a new diagnosis for her and it is explained that she will need ongoing monitoring annually for systemic complications. Other than an electrocardiogram (ECG), which of the following investigations should be requested annually?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Oesophageal manometry

Patients with systemic sclerosis may develop oesophageal reflux and swallowing problems. If the patient develops symptoms then they should be investigated with oesophageal manometry to assess dysphagia, and they may also need barium swallow to further assess them. Without symptoms, these investigations are not needed.

B High-resolution computed tomography (HR CT) chest

HR CT scan of the chest is indicated in patients with systemic sclerosis if pulmonary function tests demonstrate a restrictive picture. HR CT can then help diagnose and characterise the extent of pulmonary fibrosis.

C Pulmonary function tests and echocardiogram

This patient has systemic sclerosis and is at risk of developing complications. Complications of systemic sclerosis include: respiratory: pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension, aspiration pneumonia and pulmonary haemorrhage gastrointestinal: gastroesophageal reflux disease (GORD), peptic strictures, dysphagia, bacterial overgrowth and malabsorption renal: malignant hypertension, angiopathic haemolytic anaemia and intermittent renal crisis. Systemic sclerosis should be monitored in terms of skin and complications. Skin monitoring is done by measuring skin tightness and interlabial distance which can be combined into the Rodnan skin score. Annual monitoring for internal organ pathology includes screening for interstitial lung disease and pulmonary artery hypertension, and therefore requires pulmonary function tests, transthoracic echocardiogram and ECG on an annual basis.

D Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)

Cardiac MRI can be useful in the assessment of cardiac scleroderma, which is cardiomyopathy of the heart in the context of systemic sclerosis. This can present with shortness of breath, decreased exercise tolerance, chest pain and palpitations. Cardiac MRI is useful for patients presenting with these symptoms in the context of systemic sclerosis but is not generally used as annual monitoring.

E Right heart catheterisation

Right heart catheterisation is the gold-standard investigation to assess pulmonary arterial hypertension, a complication of systemic sclerosis. However, echocardiogram is done to screen for pulmonary hypertension and then patients who are suspected of pulmonary hypertension are further investigated with right heart

questions.question:
A 52-year-old woman presents with progressive weakness over the past two months, primarily affecting her shoulders and hips. She finds it increasingly difficult to lift objects and rise from a seated position. She denies any recent infections, respiratory symptoms or rashes. On examination, there is symmetrical proximal muscle weakness in the upper and lower limbs. There is no muscle tenderness or joint swelling. Her vital signs are normal, and systemic examination is unremarkable.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)148 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)8.1 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)350 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)40 mm/hourLess than 20 mm/hour
Creatinine (Cr)80 µmol/L60–120 µmol/L

Which investigation would best confirm a diagnosis of polymyositis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Electromyography

Electromyography (EMG) can detect muscle abnormalities typical of inflammatory myopathies such as short- duration, low-amplitude polyphasic potentials and spontaneous fibrillations. However, EMG findings are not specific to polymyositis and cannot alone confirm the diagnosis without histopathological evidence.

B Muscle biopsy

Muscle biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosing polymyositis, as it can confirm muscle inflammation, fibre necrosis and the presence of inflammatory infiltrates, all of which are characteristic of polymyositis. Muscle biopsy is essential for distinguishing polymyositis from other inflammatory and non-inflammatory muscle disorders.

C Antinuclear antibody testing

Antinuclear antibody testing can be positive in polymyositis but is non-specific, as it is also positive in various autoimmune diseases. It does not confirm polymyositis specifically and is typically used to assess associated connective tissue diseases.

D MRI of the muscles

MRI can reveal muscle oedema and inflammation, which may support the diagnosis of an inflammatory myopathy. However, it does not provide the definitive histopathological evidence needed to confirm polymyositis and is often used to guide the biopsy site rather than for diagnosis alone.

E Rheumatoid factor test

Rheumatoid factor is not typically associated with polymyositis. Its level may be elevated in patients with rheumatoid arthritis or other rheumatological diseases, but it does not contribute to a diagnosis of polymyositis.

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman attends the Emergency Department with an 8-hour history of chest pain. She reports the pain to have gradually worsened as the day continues and she is struggling to take deep breaths. The pain radiates across the front of her chest and is worsened on breathing and coughing. She has taken paracetamol for the pain which has provided only some relief. Her past medical history includes irritable bowel syndrome and fibromyalgia. She takes regular duloxetine and recently started over-the-counter vitamin supplementation after recently recovering from influenza. On examination, she is afebrile. Her heart rate is 66 bpm and regular, with a blood pressure of 123/77 mmHg. She is warm peripherally and her calves are soft and non-tender bilaterally, with no evidence of oedema. On auscultation, her heart sounds are normal and chest sounds are clear, with oxygen saturations of 98% on room air. Palpation of her anterior chest wall causes severe discomfort. She has a soft and non-tender abdomen. Chest X-ray: clear lung fields Electrocardiogram (ECG): normal sinus rhythm Bloods: pending Assuming the likely diagnosis, what is the next most appropriate step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Corticosteroids

Corticosteroid injections may play a role in reducing inflammation in costochondritis. However, they are not the first-line recommended treatment.

B Lidocaine 1% patch

Lidocaine patches are not frequently used to treat costochondritis. First-line measures such as oral analgesia should be trialled initially. Adding to this, this patient seems to have chest pain across her entire anterior chest wall requiring the need for several patches.

C Low-molecular weight heparin

Low-molecular-weight heparin is used in the treatment of venous thromboembolism (VTE) such as pulmonary embolism (PE). PE can cause pleuritic chest pain and should be considered as a differential diagnosis. From the clinical history and examination, a Wells score should be calculated for any patient with a potential diagnosis of PE. There are some missing criteria to accurately calculate a Wells score in this patient. However, the lack of hypoxia and tachycardia and the presence of soft and non-tender calves, along with reproducible chest wall pain, make the diagnosis of PE less likely.

D Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)

This patient has costochondritis characterised by tenderness of the costochondral and chondrosternal joints of the anterior chest wall. Pain may have an acute or gradual onset and can be described as sharp, aching or like a pressure sensation. Exacerbating symptoms include coughing, deep inspiration and physical activity. Before the onset of symptoms, there is often a history of recent illness or strenuous exercise. This patient’s symptoms started shortly after an illness with influenza and is reproducible on chest wall palpation, suggesting a diagnosis of costochondritis. Treatment of choice includes regular analgesia, particularly NSAIDs like ibuprofen.

E Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)

Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) plays a role in the treatment of chronic pain syndromes such as fibromyalgia. Fibromyalgia is characterised by widespread pain that can frequently fail to improve with regular analgesia. Other illnesses often coexist with fibromyalgia such as irritable bowel syndrome, tension headache and atypical chest pain. However, the onset of chest pain after a recent viral illness is less likely to be fibromyalgia and regular analgesics should be trialled before referral for CBT.

questions.question: A 24-year-old White woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 6-day history of left-knee swelling and pain. She denies trauma and has never had issues with her joints before. On further questioning, she reports feeling feverish and nauseated with lower abdominal discomfort but puts that down to menstrual cramps. Her past medical history includes coeliac disease and hypothyroidism. On examination, she has a temperature of 37.9 °C with a heart rate of 80 bpm and a BP of 125/75 mmHg. Auscultation of her chest is clear with oxygen saturations of 98% in air. Her left knee is erythematous and warm to the touch. It is swollen and immobile due to both pain and swelling. Her abdomen is mildly tender in the right upper quadrant and suprapubic regions, but there is no guarding. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Neisseria gonorrhoeae

This patient likely has disseminated gonococcal disease, given the history of acute-onset left-knee swelling associated with fever, swelling and reduced mobility. The additional symptoms of abdominal discomfort, particularly in the suprapubic and right upper quadrant, are also suggestive of gonococcal arthritis and other complications of N. gonorrhoeae infection, such as Fitz–Hugh–Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis). Disseminated gonococcal arthritis is caused by the Gram-negative organism N. gonorrhoeae for which the treatment is intravenous ceftriaxone. Gonococcal arthritis tends to affect young, healthy adults who are sexually active, and women are more frequently affected than men.

B Salmonella enterica

S. enterica is a much rarer cause of septic arthritis, and osteomyelitis and is mostly associated with patients with sickle cell anaemia. It is unlikely to be the causative organism in this patient.

C Staphylococcus aureus

S. aureus is the most common organism associated with non-gonococcal septic arthritis. Non-gonococcal arthritis is more common in the elderly population, particularly those with co-existing joint disease or prosthetic joints. In contrast, this patient is a young female making other organisms, such as N. gonorrhoeae, more likely to be the cause.

D Staphylococcus epidermidis

S. epidermidis is a commensal organism and is less likely to be the cause of septic arthritis. It is more commonly seen in patients who are immunocompromised. Nevertheless, the presentation of a young woman with symptoms and signs of an infected joint along with a history of abdominal pain is more suggestive of N. gonorrhoeae.

E Streptococcus pyogenes

S. pyogenes (group A streptococcus) is another common cause of non-gonococcal septic arthritis. Patients infected with group A streptococcus are usually very acutely unwell with signs of septic shock. It is less likely to be the causative organism in this patient.

questions.question: A 49-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of painful mouth ulcers. He also mentions intermittent diarrhoea, and occasional colicky abdominal pain. Until a year ago, his general health had been good, but he has felt generally unwell recently with diffuse aches and pains. Six months ago, he required ophthalmological investigation and treatment for anterior uveitis. At this time, he also developed superficial venous thrombophlebitis at two different venepuncture sites. Oral lesions noted on examination are shown in the photograph below: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Behçet’s disease

Recurrent painful oral aphthous ulcers are the most common lesions associated with Behçet’s disease and occur in 99.3% of cases. Genital ulcers may also be present. At least 50% of patients who have Behçet’s disease also develop gastrointestinal erosions and ulcers that may cause abdominal pain, melaena, and even perforation. This constellation of intestinal signs and symptoms may simulate Crohn’s disease and other inflammatory bowel disorders. However, a distinguishing feature between the two conditions is the phenomenon of pathergy (a condition in which minor trauma can lead to the development of further blistering lesions), which is characteristic of Behçet’s syndrome. Ocular involvement is seen in about 70% of patients; most often in the form of anterior or posterior uveitis. Other manifestations include musculoskeletal (arthralgias/arthritis in 50%); skin (erythema nodosum, acneiform lesions, thrombophlebitis, and cutaneous hypersensitivity); central and peripheral nervous system lesions; and vascular lesions. Behçet’s syndrome can involve both the arterial and venous systems, and typically presents as superficial thrombophlebitis or deep venous thrombosis. The cause and pathogenesis of Behçet’s disease remain unknown, but the tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF-alpha) pathway is likely implicated. Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous disorder that can affect multiple organs. Common manifestations include:

B Crohn’s disease

Extraintestinal involvement of Crohn’s could lead to similar symptoms; however bowel symptoms would be the predominant feature and superficial thrombophlebitis would not be typical.

C Ulcerative colitis

As with Crohn’s disease, the symptoms of ulcerative colitis (UC) may be similar but are usually intestine predominant. Additional commonly encountered extraintestinal symptoms of UC and Crohn’s disease include arthritis, erythema nodosum, and pyoderma gangrenosum.

D Coeliac disease

Coeliac disease is associated with diarrhoea, abdominal cramping and bloating. The commonest cutaneous manifestation is of dermatitis herpetiformis.

E Sarcoidosis

fatigue, loss of weight, interstitial lung disease, erythema nodosum, lupus pernio, conductive cardiac abnormalities, and uveitis.

questions.question:
A 69-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with severe tiredness, temporal headaches and jaw claudication when she tries to eat. She has a history of hypertension, for which she takes ramipril, but is otherwise well. Examination reveals a BP of 155/95 mmHg; her heart rate is 80 bpm and regular. Visual acuity is 6/6 bilaterally and visual fields are full to confrontation. She is tender over the temporal arteries bilaterally. Her weight is 98 kg.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)121 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)9.4 × 10⁹/L4–11 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)203 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)101 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)75 mm/1 hour0–10 mm/1 hour

Steroids are to be commenced. What dose of steroids is recommended?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A 1g intravenous methylprednisolone for 3 days

Here, as no visual symptoms or signs are reported, such high-dose steroids are not required.

B 60 mg prednisolone daily

The lethargy, temporal headaches and jaw claudication in combination with a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) indicate possible giant cell arteritis. Treatment should be prompt and response is usually seen in the first 48 hours, sometimes taking up to seven days. In the absence of visual symptoms, guidelines recommend oral prednisolone at a dose of 40-60 mg daily with a slow taper. The usual treatment duration is between 12- 18 months with careful observation for relapses. Patients with suspected or confirmed giant cell arteritis with visual manifestations require urgent corticosteroid therapy. No trials have been conducted in these patients with threatened vision, but it is recommended that either intravenous methylprednisolone at a dose of 500mg-1g daily for three days followed by oral prednisolone therapy or oral prednisolone at 1 mg/kg (or between 60-100 mg daily) with a taper thereafter.

C 8 mg hydrocortisone twice daily

Hydrocortisone has a much shorter half-life than prednisolone. The approximate equivalent dose of prednisolone 60mg is 240 mg of hydrocortisone daily, usually split into 3 or 4 doses. Such a prescription would only be warranted in an IV form as a temporary measure if the patient was nil by mouth or unable to eat or drink for an alternate pathology. A dose of 8mg of hydrocortisone twice daily is a huge underdosing of corticosteroids and is unlikely to control the patient’s symptoms.

D 20 mg prednisolone daily

Giant cell arteritis has a high level of morbidity. Complications include ischaemic visual failure, stroke and polymyalgia rheumatica. Although no randomised controlled trials of therapy exist, the standard dosing of patients with suspected giant cell arteritis without threatened vision is 40-60 mg prednisolone initially. A long slow taper is then undertaken. 20 mg prednisolone is unlikely to control symptoms and may result in complications.

E 1mg/kg prednisolone daily

Where vision is threatened in giant cell arteritis a larger dose of corticosteroids is urgently warranted. This is usually given in the form of pulsed methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone starting at 60 mg. Where pulsed methylprednisolone cannot be given, then 60-100mg of oral prednisolone is recommended in current guidelines. With no sign of visual symptoms or signs here, this is not required.

questions.question:
A 64-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with a second episode of acute gout over the past four months. He was given a short course of ibuprofen, and his symptoms settled over the course of a few days. Medications include ramipril, amlodipine and bendroflumethiazide. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 134/72 mmHg and a pulse of 80 bpm and regular. His body mass index (BMI) is 29 kg/m². There is clear acute gout affecting the right great toe.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)130 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.2 × 10⁹/L4–11 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)189 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine112 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Urate630 mmol/L0.1–0.4 mmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)195 mg/L0–10 mg/L
Glucose5.4 mmol/L3.5–5.5 mmol/L*

Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention with respect to reducing the chance of further gout episodes?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Allopurinol

Given this patient is taking a thiazide diuretic, stopping the diuretic is the most appropriate first-line intervention. In the event that the urate level is still raised after cessation of the thiazide, allopurinol would be the next step for long-term prophylaxis.

B Benzbromarone

Benzbromarone is available in the United Kingdom on a named patient basis, and it is a uricosuric that is usually added in to allopurinol therapy.

C Ibuprofen

While long-term ibuprofen would likely keep the patient’s symptoms at bay, it is likely to carry significant risks, given his coexisting hypertension, and should be avoided.

D Stop Bendroflumethiazide

Thiazides are known to increase the risk for acute gout because they reduce renal clearance of uric acid. As such, they increase the propensity for acute attacks of gout. It is thought that attacks of gout are triggered by a twin rise in triglyceride and uric acid levels; hence the negative impact of bendroflumethiazide on triglycerides may further increase the risk for acute episodes.

E Stop Ramipril

Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are associated with an increased risk for gout, though not to the same degree as thiazide diuretics. It is therefore appropriate to first stop bendroflumethiazide and then consider stopping ramipril if symptoms persist.

questions.question: A 45-year old woman presented with 4-month history of an erythematous rash over her cheeks, her anterior upper chest and the backs of her hands. Over the same period she had become short of breath on exertion. In the last month, she had also complained of difficulty walking up the stairs at home. General examination revealed a rash as noted above and dilated capillaries at the base of some of the fingernails. On examination of the chest, there were a few bibasal crepitations. Neurological examination revealed mild weakness of hip flexion but it was an otherwise normal exam. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Dermatomyositis

This patient has a rash which is typical for dermatomyositis. The rash over the chest probably represents the ‘V- sign’ and the rash on the back of the hands is likely to be Gottron’s papules. Proximal weakness is manifest as difficulty walking upstairs. The shortness of breath and bi-basal crepitation are likely to represent complicating interstitial lung disease.

B Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (E-GPA)

E-GPA is a systemic vasculitis of small vessels and is associated with p-ANCA. It usually occurs in persons with a history of airway allergic hypersensitivity. Eosinophilia occurs in association with systemic features such as weight loss and night sweats. Vasculitis, particularly of the peritoneal vasculature, usually occurs in the final stages of evolution of the illness.

C Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)

This case description is not at all typical of RA, which is primarily an inflammatory disease of the joints. Skin manifestations can occur occasionally in RA, including nodules, pyoderma gangrenosum, erythema nodosum and palmar erythema. Pulmonary fibrosis can also occur as a complication of RA. However, the lack of joint involvement in this case makes RA extremely unlikely.

D Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP)

This case description is not at all typical for AIP, in which the most common manifestations are abdominal pain and psychiatric disturbances.

E Systemic lupus erythematosus

Patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) can have a rash similar to that seen in dermatomyositis. The rash in SLE is photosensitive and most commonly seen in sun-exposed areas – the cheeks (i.e. a malar distribution), upper anterior and posterior chest and over the backs of the hands. Whilst not really described clearly in this case, a heliotrope (i.e. peri-orbital ring) rash, rather than a malar rash, is more typical of dermatomyositis. Despite the potential similarity of the rash, dermatomyositis is a more likely answer in this case because of the co-existing muscle weakness and suggestion of interstitial lung disease.

questions.question:
A 64-year-old man is referred to you by the Emergency Department. He presents with a diffusely warm, swollen ankle joint although he does not seem in particular pain.The swelling has been worsening gradually over the past 12 weeks. Medications include gliclazide 160 mg/day. Examination in the Emergency Department reveals a grossly deformed red, swollen right ankle.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)122 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.5 × 10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)186 × 10⁹/L150 - 400 × 10⁹/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)12 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Ankle x-rayLoss of joint margin, significant bone destruction and joint remodelling

Which one of the following interventions is most appropriate in this case?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Calcium and vitamin D

Although one facet of treatment is to ensure he is vitamin D replete, the most important part of managing a Charcot joint is to immobilise it and allow healing.

B IV Flucloxacillin

While the joint is hot and swollen, the normal C-reactive protein and white blood cell count make it unlikely that this is due to osteomyelitis, and therefore antibiotics are not indicated.

C Immobilisation in a plaster cast

This patient has Charcot arthropathy, the clue being that he is not in any pain (it is an anaesthetic joint), the foot is grossly deformed and he likely has underlying type 2 diabetes, indicated by the prescription of gliclazide. Immobilisation in a cast for 3–6 months is the treatment of choice; this is thought to be complemented by use of bisphosphonates: the reduction in bone reabsorption associated with bisphosphonates is thought to accelerate healing. Good control of blood glucose to reduce the risk of microvascular complications is associated with a decreased incidence in Charcot arthropathy, although once established it cannot be reversed.

D Surgical drainage

Although the joint appears ‘swollen’, it is actually grossly deformed due to underlying bone and the CRP is normal, making infection very unlikely, and there is no effusion to drain.

E Ibuprofen 400 mg po tds

A Charcot joint is anaesthetic and therefore not painful, as given to you in the question, and therefore neither analgesia nor anti-inflammatories is indicated.

questions.question:
A 54-year-old woman comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. She is increasingly tired and finding it difficult to both get out of a low chair and climb the stairs, such that she is restricting her up and down trips to two per day. She has noticed a rash on her face that she put down to sunburn, although even with sun block, it does not seem to be improving. She has a past history of hypothyroidism, for which she has been taking thyroxine 100 mcg/day for the past five years. On examination, her blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg and pulse 78 bpm and regular. Cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examinations are unremarkable and her body mass index (BMI) is 25 kg/m². She has a faint erythematous rash around her eyes. There is obvious proximal

myopathy affecting the shoulder muscles and hip flexors. A picture of the rash on her hands is shown below:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)129 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)7.8 × 10⁹/L4–11 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)203 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine100 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)2.1 µU/L0.17–3.2 µU/L
Glucose5.6 mmol/L3.5–5.5 mmol/L
Creatine kinase (CK)2120 IU/L23–175 IU/L
Chest X-ray (CXR): Normal

Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate therapy for her?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Azathioprine

Azathioprine is a typical second-line agent for the treatment of dermatomyositis and is used to slowly reduce the steroid dose once an initial response to therapy has been established.

B Ciclosporin

Like azathioprine, ciclosporin is a second-line agent for the treatment of dermatomyositis. It is not considered a primary intervention.

C High dose Prednisolone

The facial rash, coupled with what look like Gottron’s papules on the photograph, proximal myopathy and significantly raised CK level, is consistent with dermatomyositis. She is young with significant symptoms and therefore requires intervention with high-dose corticosteroids as the first step.

D Increased oral Thyroxine

Although hypothyroidism is recognised as a cause of proximal myopathy, the TSH level here is in the normal range, meaning that increased thyroxine dose will not be of value in improving symptoms of muscle weakness.

E Low dose Prednisolone

Low-dose prednisolone is not of value in the treatment of dermatomyositis, where a dose of 1 mg/kg/day, up to 80 mg, is recommended.

questions.question:
You review a 42-year-old woman who is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic because blood tests have shown a positive CCP antibody at > 200. Her rheumatoid factor is negative. She denies any joint pains or stiffness and examination is normal, with no evidence of synovitis. The blood test was performed as part of a health check. Her great-grandmother had rheumatoid arthritis with significant deformities at a time that unfortunately, biological therapy was not available. She smokes 30 cigarettes per day.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)137 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)4.8 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)188 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Neutrophils2.1 × 10⁹/L2.5–7.58 × 10⁹/L
Lymphocytes1.8 × 10⁹/L1.5–3.5 × 10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)10 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour
C-reactive protein (CRP)2 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)28 IU/L10–40 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)101 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)15 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Glucose5.5 mmol/L3.5–5.5 mmol/L
Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptides (Anti-CCP)2200
Rheumatoid factor (RF)Negative
Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA)Negative

What is the best management plan?
options: Nothing: reassure and discharge her from clinic
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Start methotrexate

This lady has anti-CCP antibodies and a family history of rheumatoid arthritis. She does have a higher risk of developing rheumatoid arthritis, although she does not have any synovitis currently and therefore the benefits of starting methotrexate do not outweigh the risk.

B Advise her to stop smoking

There is evidence that stopping smoking and delaying the onset of the development of arthritis in patients at risk of developing RA (such as this lady, with positive anti-CCP antibodies) can ameliorate the prognosis of patients in whom arthritic symptoms have already developed (e.g. reduce the burden of joint damage).

C Start hydroxychloroquine

Although hydroxychloroquine is the best-tolerated and least toxic DMARD, there is no evidence that patients at risk of developing RA (asymptomatic, anti-CCP positive) have any better prognosis when treated before symptoms develop.

D Nothing: reassure and discharge her from clinic

This lady is asymptomatic and could be discharged from the clinic. However, she should be informed about the effects of smoking on her joints, advised to stop smoking and to seek medical advice if she develops any symptoms of joint pains, stiffness, swelling etc.

E Work her up for anti-TNF

This lady does not fulfil criteria for a diagnosis of RA, and is certainly not eligible for biologic therapy. There is no evidence that starting therapy before the onset of symptoms changes the prognosis or course of disease.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old man from West Africa comes to the clinic for review. He had been to the Heart Failure Clinic for review some three to four weeks earlier and had been started on some new medication. He tells you that he was unable to tolerate a drug called ramipril before this because it led to ‘problems with his kidneys’. Over the past two to three weeks, he has suffered increasing fatigue, night sweats and generalised joint pains. Examination reveals a blood pressure (BP) of 112/72 mmHg and a pulse of 85 bpm and regular. Despite the joint pains, there are no signs of active synovitis. There are bibasal crackles on auscultation of the chest.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)129 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)9.8 × 10⁹/L4–11 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)174 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine119 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Antinuclear antibody (ANA)Positive
Anti-histone antibodyPositive
Anti-RoNegative
Rheumatoid factorNegative

Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Bendroflumethiazide

Anti-Ro antibodies are often positive in drug-induced lupus related to thiazide diuretics, and so the fact that anti-Ro is negative here makes bendroflumethiazide less likely as the underlying cause.

B Bisoprolol

There are case reports of drug-induced lupus in association with beta-blocker therapy, although they would not be considered a likely cause here. The main concern is, of course, bronchospasm and worsening of asthma in association with their use.

C Furosemide

Like bisoprolol, furosemide is more rarely described as a cause of drug-induced lupus, compared to hydralazine. It is most often described as an exacerbating factor, alongside other drugs known to cause lupus themselves.

D Hydralazine

The pattern of symptoms, coupled with the autoantibody screen seen here, is suggestive of drug-induced lupus. Patients with heart failure who cannot tolerate angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibition are recommended to trial hydralazine and nitrate as alternatives, which leaves hydralazine as the most likely cause of drug-induced lupus here. Withdrawal of the drug is likely to lead to resolution of symptoms over the course of a few weeks. Other causes of drug-induced lupus include thiazides, although anti-Ro antibodies will be positive, and procainamide, isoniazid, timolol and phenytoin.

E Isosorbide mononitrate

Nitrates are not described as a cause of drug-induced lupus and are effective in reducing preload in patients with cardiac failure.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old Turkish man is referred with a suspected deep vein thrombosis (DVT) to the Emergency Department by his General Practitioner (GP). He recently returned to the United Kingdom after a 1-year break in Turkey. While away, he was admitted once to the hospital with diarrhoea and abdominal pain, which was accompanied by multiple painful lesions in his mouth. A few days after discharge from the hospital, he presented again to the Emergency Department with an acute red and painful eye. He was sent home with eye drops for suspected conjunctivitis. A few months afterwards, the mouth lesions reappeared, but this time with similar lesions on his scrotum. At the same time, his ankle and wrist joints were swollen and painful. The lesions resolved after a few weeks, as well as the joint problems. He has no past medical history. On examination, he is pyrexial with a temperature of 38 °C. The left calf is swollen and tender, and there are several painful lesions on the extensor surface of both legs. The wrists and ankles are swollen and tender, and there are two well-demarcated ulcers on the roof of his mouth that are tender to touch.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Rheumatoid factor (RF)Negative
Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA)Negative
Haemoglobin (Hb)88 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)14.0 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)350 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.8 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea8.8 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)98 μmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)120 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour
C-reactive protein (CRP)210 g/L< 10 g/L
Doppler ultrasound (US)Popliteal deep vein thrombosis (DVT)

Given the likely diagnosis, what is the best management option for this patient?
options: Adalimumab 80 mg initially, with 40-mg dose after two weeks
Apixaban 10 mg twice a day for seven days, followed by 5 mg twice a day
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Adalimumab 80 mg initially, with 40-mg dose after two weeks

Venous thrombotic events are managed in Behçet syndrome by controlling inflammation with a combination of corticosteroids and immunosuppressants such as azathioprine, cyclophosphamide or ciclosporin.

B Apixaban 10 mg twice a day for seven days, followed by 5 mg twice a day

Venous thrombotic events are managed in Behçet syndrome by controlling inflammation with a combination of corticosteroids and immunosuppressants such as azathioprine, cyclophosphamide or ciclosporin. This is therefore the correct option from those listed. A Rheumatology specialist should be involved in this case to guide immunosuppressant choice and the need for anticoagulation treatment.

C Enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg/day

Tumour necrosis factor-alpha inhibitors can be considered for severe Behçet syndrome and refractory venous thrombosis. However, they would be given in combination with corticosteroids, and therefore, this does not represent the best treatment option.

D Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day and azathioprine 2.5 mg/kg/day

This man has orogenital ulceration, likely uveitis, inflammation in his bowels, erythema nodosum and a deep vein thrombosis (DVT), unprovoked as the flight to Turkey is not long-haul. Behçet syndrome is characterised predominantly by inflammation of small blood vessels, leading to recurrent ulceration, especially in the oral and genital mucosa. It persists for many years, with characteristic painful oral and genital ulcers, uveitis, seronegative arthritis, thrombophlebitis, DVT and erythema nodosum.

E Prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day

Anticoagulants may be used in some patients, if the overall bleeding risk is low and coexisting pulmonary artery aneurysms are ruled out; however, they are not part of the standard treatment approach. A specialist consultation should be completed for the choice of anticoagulant therapy in patients with Behçet syndrome. Steroid therapy alone is not the recommended management. A specialist consultation should be completed to guide the choice of immunosuppressant in combination with prednisolone

questions.question:
A 43-year-old woman is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. Her GP had observed Raynaud’s phenomenon, calcinosis and thickening of the skin affecting her fingers, and telangiectasiae around her mouth and over her upper body. Her provisional diagnosis was systemic sclerosis. You confirm the clinical features on examination, and her BP is 155/82 mmHg.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)131 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)7.2 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)199 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)122 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
ANA+
Anti-RNA polymerase III antibody+
UrineProtein+

Which of the following is she at risk of developing?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A CREST syndrome

CREST syndrome is a term no longer used, as not all patients fulfil the entire mnemonic. Rather, the ‘limited cutaneous’ terminology is preferred.

B Features of rheumatoid arthritis

Even if she had a rheumatoid factor (RF), this is non-specific and does not indicate propensity to develop features of rheumatoid arthritis.

C Limited cutaneous disease only

Anti-centromere antibodies are usually associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis, and these patients are more likely to have pulmonary hypertension and gastrointestinal involvement.

D Pulmonary fibrosis

Anti-Scl-70 antibody is generally associated with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and a higher risk of severe interstitial lung disease.

E Scleroderma renal crisis

Different auto-antibody patterns are associated with differing patterns of disease associated with systemic sclerosis. Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) tests positive in approximately 95% of patients with SSc, and therefore a negative test should prompt consideration of other fibrosing illnesses. Anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies are found in patients with diffuse disease, and are associated with rapidly progressive skin involvement as well as an increased risk for scleroderma renal crisis. These patients may also be at increased risk for cancer.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man presents to the Respiratory Clinic with complaints of a non-productive cough and exertional dyspnoea that has been progressive over the past two years. He smokes ten cigarettes per day and consumes alcohol occasionally. He reports normal bowel activity but has had to urinate more frequently and has felt increasingly thirsty over the past six months. The patient also has back pain, with difficulty bending forward for the past four months. On examination, bilateral crepitations were present in the apical region of both lung fields. His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg and his heart rate is 104 bpm. Oximetry revealed an oxygen saturation of 92% on room air. Which of the following investigations would confirm the diagnosis in this patient?
options: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of hip and spine with human leukocyte antigen (HLA) B-27 testing
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage

Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage can help in the diagnosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis. However, its main utility lies in eliminating infections and other infiltrating disorders that can be seen in young adults.

B Cytology for malignant cells

Cytology for malignancy is neither sensitive nor specific and cannot be used for the diagnosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis.

C High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) thorax

While HRCT thorax would be useful in delineating the underlying pulmonary pathology, it is not useful in confirming the diagnosis. In this patient who is a young smoker with interstitial lung disease, vertebral involvement and features of diabetes insipidus, the likely diagnosis is Langerhans cell histiocytosis. In these patients, HRCT thorax may show multiple apical cystic lesions, nodules, cavitating nodules and, in late stages, honeycombing of the lung.

D Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of hip and spine with human leukocyte antigen (HLA) B-27 testing

Hip and spine MRI will be helpful in the diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis, which can also present with apical lung fibrosis and cause back pain. However, the patient’s polyuria and polydipsia likely indicate diabetes insipidus and this is not likely to be caused by ankylosing spondylitis.

E Transbronchial lung biopsy

A lung biopsy forms the mainstay of diagnosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis. Identification of Langerhans cells, which are moderately sized with an irregular convoluted nucleus, is typical. Immunohistochemical staining of the biopsy specimen and positivity for CD1a and S100 are confirmatory. Additionally, electron microscopy may be useful for confirmation by identification of Birbeck granules.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old man with a history of diabetes presented to the clinic with bilateral knee pain. He works as an insurance salesman; he is a non-smoker but drinks on most weekends. He is on insulin for the diabetes and also takes sildenafil occasionally for erectile dysfunction. On examination, he appeared suntanned with sparse body hair. The knees were swollen and tender, with limited range of movement.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Sodium (Na⁺)135 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.0 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)110 μmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Albumin35 g/L35 - 55 g/L
Bilirubin1.75 mg/dl0.2 - 1.2 mg/dl
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)75 U/L7 - 55 U/L
Aspartate transaminase (AST)65 U/L10 - 40 U/L
Gamma glutamyl-transferase (GGT)160 U/L< 50 U/L
Glucose14 mmol/L3.9 - 7.1 mmol/L
Luteinising hormone (LH)0.6 U/L1.25 - 7.80 U/L (male)
Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)0.5 U/L1.0 - 7.0 U/L
Testosterone6.8 nmol/l9.0 - 35.0 nmol/l
X-ray of the kneesCalcification present

What is the most likely cause of the joint abnormality?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Osteomalacia

Ochronosis describes the pigment deposition that occurs in the connective tissues of patients with alkaptonuria, an autosomal recessive disorder. Brown or blue–grey discoloration of the skin can be seen in the axillary and inguinal areas, face, palms or soles. The bronze appearance of the skin in this patient with the associated signs is not typical for alkaptonuria.

B Ochronosis

Cystinosis is a metabolic disease caused by the accumulation of cysteine, characteristically causing end-stage renal function.

C Cystinosis

Bilateral knee involvement would be unusual for gout, which would present with hot, tender, swollen joints.

D Chondrocalcinosis

Hereditary haemochromatosis should be suspected in patients with liver cirrhosis (liver function tests can often be normal), diabetes mellitus, hypogonadism and impotence, skin hyperpigmentation, fatigue and arthropathy. Biochemical findings include high serum iron, ferritin and transferrin saturation, and liver biopsy shows staining for excess iron. Arthropathy in hereditary haemochromatosis is due to calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition and can include pseudo-gout, chondrocalcinosis and chronic arthropathy. Bilateral knee joint pain is not a common presentation of osteomalacia, which is often asymptomatic. Bone pain and tenderness, fragility fractures, waddling gait and osteopenia on X-ray may be features.

E Gout

Imaging findings could include subcortical bone cysts. Monosodium urate crystal deposition is not associated with hereditary haemochromatosis.

questions.question:
A 66-year-old man presents with bony pain affecting his right hip and pelvis. He has a past history of prostatism, for which he received a transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) some three years earlier. On examination, there is pain on right hip flexion and internal and external rotation.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)121 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)5.0 × 10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)191 × 10⁹/L150 - 400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.6 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)145 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Corrected calcium (Ca²⁺)2.3 mmol/L2.2 - 2.7 mmol/L
Prostate-specific antigen (PSA)2.0 μg/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)360 U/L30 - 150 U/L
X-ray of the pelvis is shown below.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Metastatic prostatic carcinoma

It is likely that his previous TURP was for benign prostatic hypertrophy. His PSA level now does not give any cause for concern and his calcium level is normal.

B Osteoarthritis of the right hip

X-rays of osteoarthritis show sclerosis, without areas of osteolysis. The isolated elevated ALP level also fits with Paget’s disease.

C Myeloma

His calcium level is normal; the ALP level is elevated, and there are areas of increased bone density on the X- ray, a picture that does not fit with myeloma.

D Paget’s disease of bone

The X-ray shows severe degenerative disease in the right hip, along with cortical thickening. As is most common in the general population, these changes are found more so in the right hip than the left. The site described is a typical one for Paget’s disease, and the combination of raised alkaline phosphatase and normal calcium level also fits with this. A radionucleotide bone scan may be useful at a later stage to determine the extent of disease. Both a prolonged oral course of bisphosphonates and intermittent intravenous courses are used for the treatment of Paget’s disease. These inhibit osteolysis and, as such, lead to a reduction in serum ALP levels (which can be used for serial measurements of treatment response) and reduce the pain associated with Paget’s disease. For patients who fail to respond to bisphosphonates or cannot tolerate them, calcitonin may be a suitable alternative.

E Hyperparathyroidism

His calcium level is normal.

questions.question:
A 59-year-old woman with a long history of asthma comes to the clinic for review. She previously had a myocardial infarction, aged 51. She is currently taking 500 μg fLuticasone inhaled bd and salbutamol prn. She complains of a further exacerbation and you prescribe her oral prednisolone. This is her eighth course of oral steroids over the past 3 years. Other past medical history of note includes vertebral fractures diagnosed after an episode of acute pain some 3 months ago. On auscultation of her chest you can hear wheeze throughout both lung fields.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin123 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)5.3 × 10⁹/L4–11 × 10⁹/L
Platelets201 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine120 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
eGFR57
T score – 2.6

Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy for her osteoporosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Teriparatide

Guidelines recommend a weekly oral bisphosphonate first, before an alternative of a different frequency.

B Ibandronate

Ibandronate is given intravenously every 3 months.

C Alendronate

Guidelines for osteoporosis recommend prescription of a weekly generic bisphosphonate in the first instance. For patients who fail to tolerate a weekly preparation, monthly oral or more intermittent IV preparations may be appropriate. Strontium and teriparatide are reserved for patients with more severe osteoporosis. Her asthma therapy should be reviewed, with consideration of a long acting beta agonist. See also SIGN guideline on osteoporosis. This patient is on glucocorticoids and has a fragility fracture (vertebral) and is osteoporotic on her DEXA scan (T score <–2.5). She therefore does need therapy and bone protection and calcium and vitamin D is insufficient on its own.

D Strontium

Strontium is relatively contraindicated in patients with previous myocardial infarctions, or other thromboembolic diseases (eg pulmonary emboli) as it can increase the thrombotic risk.

E Calcium and vitamin D

While teriparatide does have some evidence for osteoporotic vertebral fractures, current NICE guidelines recommend bisphonates first and teriparatide is reserved for more severe osteoporosis.

questions.question:
A 51-year-old man, who owns a bar in Tenerife, comes to the Emergency Department for review. He has suffered increasingly severe knee pains and is now unable to bend his right knee due to pain and swelling. He admits to drinking up to 10 units of alcohol per day and has recently been recommended to follow a diabetic diet by his Spanish general practitioner. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 155/95 mmHg and a pulse of 80 bpm and regular. He is tanned, in keeping with living in Spain. There is truncal obesity, with a body mass index (BMI) of 33 kg/m². Both knees are swollen, the right more so than the left, and flexion of the right knee is limited to around 30 degrees.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)134 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)8.0 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)200 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)42 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)110 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Glucose10.9 mmol/L3.5–5.5 mmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)122 IU/L7–55 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)95 IU/L30–150 IU/L
Ferritin630 µg/L24–355 µg/L (male)
Urate0.43 mmol/L0.1–0.4 mmol/L (male)

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Gout

There are multiple features in the history which point towards a diagnosis of pseudogout over osteoarthritis, though it is an important differential. The joint X-ray would help distinguish between the two diagnoses.

B Osteoarthritis

Pseudogout has the classical chondrocalcinosis appearance, whereas in osteoarthritis, patients have loss of joint space, osteophyte formation, subchondral sclerosis and subchondral cysts on X-ray.

C Pseudogout

This patient presents with oligoarthritis and has evidence of chronic liver disease with abnormal liver function tests and elevated ferritin and blood glucose levels. This constellation of features supports an underlying diagnosis of haemochromatosis, which is associated with pseudogout or pyrophosphate arthropathy. While uric acid levels are commonly measured in patients with suspected gout, it is not very sensitive or specific, as 15% of patients with gout have normal serum uric acid levels while 25% of the normal population have hyperuricaemia. Given the other features present, pseudogout is the more likely underlying diagnosis, as opposed to gout.

D Septic arthritis

Given the WCC is normal and CRP level is only 42, septic arthritis seems very unlikely. The chronic nature of this patient’s condition also makes septic arthritis less likely in this scenario.

E Seronegative arthritis

The lack of involvement of joints other than the knees makes the diagnosis of seronegative arthritis less likely.

questions.question: A 34-year-old sales representative presents with severe pain going down her neck and right arm. She admits that this pain is worse on sitting in her car while driving for long periods. Past history includes two previous road traffic accidents, but nil else of note. On examination, there is weakness and sensory loss over a C5/C6 nerve distribution and pain with neck movement, particularly extension. An MRI of the spinal cord is arranged. Which other investigation would be most useful in this case?
options: Plain X-rays of the right elbow
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Nerve conduction studies

This patient has symptoms of cervical radiculopathy, resulting from disc degeneration due either to herniation or degenerative change (spondylosis). When there are posterior osteophytes leading to anterior spinal cord compression, as is likely here, patients present with chronic radicular arm pain, numbness and tingling sensations. The investigation of choice is magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanning to assess spinal cord encroachment, and nerve conduction studies to assess the degree of nerve damage. Treatment is with physiotherapy and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents. Patients will usually improve with time, and surgical intervention is needed in less than 5% of patients.

B Myelogram

Myelography uses a real-time form of X-ray called fluoroscopy and an injection of contrast material to evaluate the spinal cord, nerve roots and spinal lining (meninges). It is particularly useful for assessing the spine following surgery, and also for assessing disc abnormalities in patients who cannot undergo MRI. A myelogram is not appropriate here as it is invasive and expensive, and there are no contraindications to an MRI in this case.

C Autoimmune profile

This lady has a likely mechanical problem, with no features to suggest an autoimmune/inflammatory cause.

D Arthroscopy of the right shoulder

This lady has a cervical radiculopathy, i.e. nerves emanating from the cervical spine, and therefore a shoulder arthroscopy is unlikely to help.

E Plain X-rays of the right elbow

The C5/C6 radiculopathy is not related to her elbow. The ulnar nerve is often compressed at the elbow, however.

questions.question: A 54-year-old man presents to his general practitioner (GP) complaining that he is unable to get up off his low sofa. There is also a history of pain and tenderness particularly over the thigh muscles and the shoulder girdle. On further questioning, he admits to shortness of breath on exercise and chronic cough. Examination reveals an obese man with obvious proximal muscle weakness and evidence of interstitial lung disease. CK level is 1050 U/l (24–195), ESR is raised and anti-Jo-1 antibodies are positive. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Polymyalgia rheumatica

PMR is characterised by bilateral aching and morning stiffness in at least two areas (neck or torso, shoulders or proximal arms, hips or thighs). There is elevated ESR and a prompt response to low-dose glucocorticoids. The history of pain and tenderness and the additional symptoms are not consistent with PMR.

B Dermatomyositis

Dermatomyositis and polymyositis are both idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, but the former is distinguished by the presence of cutaneous lesions such as Gottron’s papules, heliotrope rash or the shawl sign.

C Polymyositis

Patients with polymyositis commonly present after 3–6 months of symptoms with painful proximal muscle weakness. CK levels may be elevated to 5–50 times the upper limit of normal. Anti-Jo-1 antibodies are associated with coexistent interstitial lung disease, Raynaud’s phenomenon and peripheral arthritis. Prednisolone is the mainstay of treatment, at an initial dose of 1 mg/kg/day. In patients who fail to show improvement, disease-modifying steroid-sparing agents may be added. A high-protein diet and supervised exercise may further improve symptoms. Most patients have a favourable response to corticosteroid therapy, and 5-year survival rates approach 80%. Women are more frequently affected than men, with a female:male ratio of 3:1. There is an association with malignancy in a significant minority of patients, including adenocarcinomas of the cervix, lung, ovaries, pancreas, bladder and stomach.

D Giant cell arteritis

The lack of unilateral headache/scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and the rise in CK make GCA unlikely.

E Hypothyroidism

Hypothyroidism should always be ruled out in patients presenting with a possible myopathy, but hypothyroid- related myopathy is not associated with a high rise in CK or anti-Jo antibodies.

questions.question:
A-40-year old man presents to the Emergency Department with digital ulceration and areas of gangrene affecting the fingers and toes. The problem started a few months back with insidious tingling, numbness and discolouration of his fingers associated with pain. Gradually, the symptoms progressed with more severe discolouration and the appearance of ulcers on the tip of his fingers associated with a constant burning sensation. He noticed that on walking he would experience severe pain in the instep of his foot and the calves. There is no history of angina or exertional dyspnoea. He is a heavy smoker but has no medical history. Examination revealed cold hands and feet with extensive cyanosis, ulceration and gangrene of the fingers and toes. There are absent pulses in the radial, dorsalis pedis and posterior tibia arteries.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)126 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)12.0 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)240 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)135 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)80 μmol/L50–120 μmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)20 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour
Rheumatoid factor (RF)Negative
Antinuclear antibody (ANA)Absent

What is the underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Takayasu’s arteritis

There is no constitutional upset, or signs of large vessel and aortic involvement, inflammatory markers are normal and Takayasu’s usually occurs in females.

B Disseminated atherosclerosis

There is no history of angina or exertional dyspnoea.

C Systemic sclerosis

The patient has negative autoantibodies and has no other features of systemic sclerosis.

D Buerger’s disease

This heavy smoker has critical digital ischaemia with absent pulses and negative autoantibodies. Thrombangiitis obliterans (Buerger’s disease) is a disease of small and medium-sized arteries and veins resulting in inflammation and ulceration. There is no excessive atheroma and it does not involve the coronary arteries like atherosclerosis. The disease occurs mainly in cigarette smokers. The patient presents with symptoms of arterial ischaemia. Migratory phlebitis in the superficial vein is present in 40% of cases. The disease progresses proximally, resulting in gangrene of the digits. Diagnosis is usually clinical. Arteriogram is also of benefit and will show occlusion of distal arteries of the hands and feet. Treatment is supportive and patients should stop smoking.

E Acrocyanosis

Acrocyanosis is persistent blue or cyanotic discoloration of the extremities, most commonly occurring in the hands, although it also occurs in the feet and distal parts of face. Acrocyanosis is not painful, nor is it associated with digital ulceration.

questions.question: A 43-year-old man attends for review. His past medical history includes renal stones treated by lithotripsy, and he also has type 2 diabetes. He is taking treatment for high cholesterol. He has been attending the clinic for a number of months with long-standing pain and swelling in his fingers. This is the clinical appearance of his hands: Picture courtesy of Charlie Goldberg, M.D., UCSD School of Medicine and VA Medical Center, San Diego, CA What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Calcinosis

Calcinosis cutis is the deposition of insoluble calcium salts in the skin and subcutaneous tissue. White calcium deposits can be seen in nodules, unlike the picture shown here.

B Gout

This is chronic gout with tophi (uric acid crystals in the soft tissues), indicating long-standing hyperuricaemia. Untreated chronic tophaceous gout can develop and lead to severe joint destruction. Men are affected twice as commonly as women, and it tends to be a disease of middle to older age; as a general rule, uric acid levels are elevated for 20 years before the onset of gout. Hyperuricaemia is associated with an increase in all-cause mortality. Patients with gout are often clustered within the metabolic syndrome: diabetes, hypertension, hypertriglyceridaemia and low high-density lipoproteins, though no evidence indicates that either gout or hyperuricaemia causes any of these other disorders. The relationship between serum uric acid and cardiovascular disease remains controversial, but raised uric acid may be an independent risk factor for vascular disease in some individuals with other risk factors.

C Pseudo-gout

The clinical manifestations of the crystal arthropathies can be difficult to distinguish. However, pseudo-gout tends to occur in older patients and risk factors include hypothyroidism, haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism and Wilson’s disease. Furthermore, there are risk factors for gout in this patient.

D Psoriatic arthropathy

Psoriatic arthropathy most commonly presents as a poly- or oligoarthritis. There are five patterns of involvement: distal arthritis (DIP joint involvement), asymmetric oligoarthritis, symmetric polyarthritis, arthritis mutilans and spondyloarthritis. This is not the description provided for this patient.

E Rheumatoid arthritis

The swelling is more extensive than would be expected for RA, and there is no history of joint stiffness in the history, which makes RA unlikely.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old woman, known to have stable rheumatoid arthritis for 20 years, has been re-referred to the Rheumatology Clinic with symptoms of chronic foul-smelling diarrhoea. She says she has lost 10 kg in weight in last 6 months. Her general appetite is quite poor as well. She finds herself quite lethargic and has noticed peripheral oedema early in the mornings. According to her, her joints have not troubled her for a long time. She is currently on methotrexate and folic acid. On examination, she has waxy skin, with plaques clustered in the axillary folds, and multiple bruises are seen. No lymph nodes are palpable. Joint examination showed no evidence of synovitis. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm, blood pressure (BP) 140/90 mmHg and respiratory rate (RR) 16 breaths/min. Heart sounds are normal, and she has good air entry bilaterally, with no added sounds. Abdominal examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly. There is no ascites, and no other masses are felt. Central nervous system examination shows evidence of peripheral neuropathy.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Sodium (Na⁺)143 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Urea7.8 mmol/L2.5 - 6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)120 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Liver function testsNormal
Thyroid function testsNormal
C-reactive protein (CRP)20 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)9 mm/h1 - 22 mm/h
24-h urinary analysisShows 5 g of proteinuria
Chest X–rayShows an enlarged cardiac silhouette
Electrocardiogram (ECG)Shows low-voltage QRS complexes

Which one of the following will be of most diagnostic value?
options: Serial sputum samples for acid-fast bacilli and tuberculosis (TB) culture
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy

Bone marrow aspirate may reveal amyloid deposits, but it is significantly more invasive, when compared to a rectal biopsy, and is therefore not the preferred option.

B Serial sputum samples for acid-fast bacilli and tuberculosis (TB) culture

Given respiratory examination is normal and there are no symptoms of cough, TB is unlikely as the cause of her current symptoms.

C Rectal biopsy

This patient has many of the hallmarks of systemic amyloidosis. An abdominal fat biopsy or a rectal biopsy is the best way to make the diagnosis. A positive Congo red histological stain helps to establish diagnosis. The AA type of amyloid is seen secondary to a host of chronic inflammatory conditions, including long-standing rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis, bronchiectasis, familial Mediterranean fever, and leprosy. Amyloidosis should be suspected in any patient with an underlying chronic inflammatory disease who develops hepatosplenomegaly, malabsorption, cardiac disease or proteinuria. Cardiac disease usually consists of congestive heart failure with low QRS-complex voltage and exquisite sensitivity to digitalis. Echocardiography shows a characteristic speckled appearance and may also be helpful in contributing to the diagnostic process. Waxy papules in the axillary folds may signal the deposition of amyloid in the skin; purpura after minor skin trauma is not uncommon. In addition to amyloid-induced synovitis, peripheral neuropathy and carpal tunnel syndrome may be seen.

D Nerve conduction studies

Although nerve conduction studies are likely to be abnormal as a result of amyloidosis, they will not provide a histological diagnosis.

E Faecal elastase

Faecal elastase is used as a screening test for pancreatic insufficiency, and although malabsorption is suspected, there may be other reasons for it to occur here such as bacterial overgrowth due to gut dysmotility.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man presents to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. He complains of multiple joint pains, particularly affecting his back, wrists, ankles and feet, with clear distal interphalangeal joint involvement. On examination, he has psoriatic patches on his elbows. There is onycholysis, transverse ridging and pitting on examination of his nails. DIP swelling, pain and restricted movement is noted. He is started on and methotrexate but on return to the clinic there is no improvement. You elect to treat him with adalimumab. The mode of action of adalimumab is mediated through which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A C-reactive protein (CRP)

While CRP and ESR may well fall in response to anti-TNF therapy, they are more non-specific markers of inflammation.

B Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)

While CRP and ESR may well fall in response to anti-TNF therapy, they are more non-specific markers of inflammation.

C IL-23

Ustekinumab has recently been approved by NICE for the treatment of psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis, and is an IL-12/23 antagonist.

D TNF-α

Adalimumab is anti-TNF-α monoclonal antibody. Adalimumab, etanercept and infliximab are anti-TNF agents which show some degree of efficacy as second-line agents in the management of psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis. TNF-α is thought to play an important role as a cytokine leading to worsening of joint inflammation and destruction.

E IL-12

Ustekinumab has recently been approved by NICE for the treatment of psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis, and is an IL-12/23 antagonist.

questions.question:
You are seeing a 54-year-old woman in the clinic. She has had rheumatoid arthritis (RA) for the past 4 years and is on treatment with methotrexate 20 mg per week. She complains of pain in the joints of the both hands with tingling/numbness over the thumb and lateral two fingers, these being present for the last 6 months. The pain in her joints is present all the time and is worse in the mornings. Paraesthesia occurs intermittently and awakens her in the night. Examination reveals mild swelling and tenderness over the small joints of the hands and wrists. There is no motor or sensory deficit on neurological examination.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)114 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)9.6 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)234 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)38 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour
C-reactive protein (CRP)11 mg/L< 0 mg/L

What would be the most appropriate further investigation at this stage?
options: Urgent magnetic resonance (MR) scan of the cervical spine
Routine MR of the cervical spine
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Urgent magnetic resonance (MR) scan of the cervical spine

This lady has carpal tunnel syndrome, where the median nerve is usually compressed at the wrist. Cervical spine imaging is not indicated.

B Routine MR of the cervical spine

This lady has carpal tunnel syndrome, where the median nerve is usually compressed at the wrist. Cervical spine imaging is not indicated.

C X-ray of the hands

X-rays are not helpful in the diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome or assessing RA disease activity, but may be useful in detecting damage resulting from RA.

D MR of the hands

MRI imaging of the hands may not show median nerve compression. It is very expensive and an insensitive method for detection of carpal tunnel syndrome. MR imaging may be helpful in looking for RA disease activity, although an ultrasound is cheaper and faster (but less sensitive).

E Electromyogram (EMG)/nerve conduction studies

This patient has carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS), as evident by paraesthesia in the hands especially at night. CTS occurs as a result of compression of the median nerve at the wrist and characteristically affects the thumb and lateral two fingers. It is seen commonly in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), most often due to entrapment of the median nerve by synovial swelling. Treatment includes the use of resting hand splints, local corticosteroid injections or median nerve release surgery. An electromyogram (EMG)/nerve conduction study is useful for confirming clinical diagnosis prior to actual surgery.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman who is being treated with methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis has misunderstood the directions for therapy and presents to the surgery with glossitis, severe mouth ulcers and megaloblastic anaemia. On further questioning, it transpires she has been taking a dose of 40 mg per week, rather than 10 mg per week.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)98 g/L115–155 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)107 fL76–98 fL
White cell count (WCC)2.3 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)95 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate rescue medication?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Vitamin B12

Vitamin B12 deficiency can occur with decreased intake, e.g. veganism; decreased absorption, e.g. Crohn’s disease, coeliac disease, pancreatic insufficiency or pernicious anaemia; or with drugs that interfere with absorption such as metformin, antihistamines and proton pump inhibitors (PPIs). Vitamin B12 deficiency causes macrocytic anaemia, jaundice, mental sluggishness and a shuffling gait. This is similar to the presentation of folate deficiency, but vitamin B12 deficiency occurs over years, while folate deficiency develops over months. The history of high dose methotrexate makes vitamin B12 deficiency less likely than folate deficiency.

B Folinic acid

Folinic acid is the correct answer. Medication errors with respect to rheumatoid arthritis are not uncommon. Patients occasionally find it difficult to understand that they must take methotrexate weekly, as opposed to daily. Calcium folinate is a potent antagonist for the effects of methotrexate on the haematopoietic system, given by intravenous (IV) infusion at doses of up to 75 mg in the first 12 hours. This can then be followed by doses of 6–12 mg every 4 hours. Blood transfusion may also be required in exceptional circumstances. Where a massive overdose of methotrexate has occurred, hydration and urinary alkalinisation may be an option. Standard dialysis is ineffective in removing methotrexate, although intermittent high-flux dialysis may be of value.

C Vitamin C

Vitamin C, or ascorbic acid, deficiency causes scurvy. This is characterised by primarily cutaneous findings, including petechiae, bruising, perifollicular bleeding, gingivitis and arthralgia. Deficiency is primarily due to dietary lack of fruits and vegetables. It is primarily seen in patients with drug or alcohol dependence or in severe malnourishment.

D Iron sulfate

Iron deficiency can occur primarily due to decreased dietary intake, reduced absorption and blood loss. Presentation can include symptoms of anaemia, e.g. fatigue, weakness and angina pectoris, and signs such as pallor, cheilosis and koilonychia. There is no particular cause for the loss in this patient, and anaemia would be far more likely to be microcytic, rather than macrocytic, in nature.

E Niacin

Niacin, or vitamin B3, deficiency causes a condition called pellagra. This is characterised by photosensitive pigmented dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia. Pellagra tends to occur in patients with malabsorption and in those with alcohol dependence. The absence of such clinical findings makes this an unlikely diagnosis and treatment.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old white man presented with a 2-week history of fever and chills followed by a widespread papular rash over his body. One week ago, he noticed that his wrist and ankle were swollen and tender. The inflammation resolved a few days later, but now his right knee is very swollen and tender and he can barely weight-bear on it. He works as a computer salesman and he was in Thailand until 2 weeks ago on a business trip. On examination, his right knee is hot and swollen and there are a few pustular lesions on his trunk.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)136 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)13.0 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)145 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5–5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)88 μmol/L50–120 μmol/L
Rheumatoid factor (RF)Negative
Antinuclear antibody (ANA)Absent
Synovial fluid white cells> 20 000/μl

What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Acute gout

The age, social history and associated signs are not typical for acute gout, which usually presents as a mono- arthritis.

B Reactive arthritis

Reactive arthritis would be in the differential diagnosis, but the presence of white cells in the synovial fluid indicates joint infection rather than an inflammatory response to remote infection, as is the case in reactive arthritis.
