Reactive arthritis also typically presents with the triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis and urethritis.

C Gonococcal arthritis

Disseminated gonococcal infection is caused by the bacteraemic spread of the sexually transmitted bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The syndrome described in this patient is the dermatitis–polyarthritis–tenosynovitis syndrome, symptoms including fever, symmetrical polyarthralgia (small or large joints), tenosynovitis and dermatitis (painless vesiculopustular lesions). Diagnosis is made by culture of synovial fluid, skin lesions and specimens from urethral swabs. Treatment includes symptomatic relief with NSAIDs and ceftriaxone and azithromycin.

D Tuberculous arthritis

TB arthritis tends to occur in the knee and hip, which is subacute in onset. It is uncommon in developed countries and would not explain the associated signs.

E Pseudo-gout

The age, social history and associated signs are not typical for pseudo-gout, which usually presents as a mono- arthritis.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old woman with a history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presents with right-sided pleural chest pain and a dry cough, which she has had for 3 weeks. On examination, she is apyrexial. Auscultation of the chest reveals normal breath sounds although shallow respiration is noted. Chest X-ray is normal. On further questioning, she reveals that her SLE is usually well controlled and that all her SLE tests were normal when she was seen in clinic 3 months ago.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
C-Reactive protein (CRP)8 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Serum Immunoglobulin G (IgG)16.0 g/L6.0–13.0 g/L
Complement C90 mg/dl65–190 mg/dl
Complement C10 mg/dl15–50 mg/dl
p (O )11.5 kPa10.5–13.5 kPa
p (CO )4.8 kPa4.6–6.0 kPa
Oxygen saturation98%

What is the most likely diagnosis? a a
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Reactivation of SLE

Systemic lupus erythematosus is a relapsing and remitting non-organ-specific autoimmune disease characterised by vasculitis and the presence of antinuclear antibodies. Respiratory symptoms are common (in 65%), and these include non-infective pleurisy. Cases of pneumonia are also more common than in the general population due to a relative immune paresis. Early markers of SLE disease activity include falling C levels, although congenital C deficiency is itself a predisposing factor for SLE development, so these tests must be interpreted with caution. Other markers of disease activity include rising immunoglobulins, falling haemoglobin (Hb), white cell count (WCC), platelets and albumin.

B Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP)

PCP is an opportunistic infection associated with immunosuppression due to HIV, haematological disorders (especially leukaemia and post-bone marrow transplant) and oncology and renal transplantation. A decrease in oxygen saturation, as measured by pulse-oximetry during exercise, indicates PCP, especially when the patient doesn’t appear acutely unwell and with minimal symptoms.

C Pneumonia

Pneumonia is an unlikely diagnosis as there are no focal chest signs and CXR is normal. Pathogenic infection of the lungs presents with a productive cough and signs of hyperthermia, tachypnoea and tachycardia, with altered mental status.

D Pulmonary embolus (PE)

PE may present with the similar symptoms, but ABG results may show reduced PaO and PaCO . The classic findings are not useful in the diagnosis of PE. Many conditions also cause hypoxaemia, but hypocapnia usually is present with embolism; hypercapnia, on the other hand, is rare. A massive PE may show combined respiratory and metabolic acidosis due to circulatory collapse.

E Costochondritis

This condition is diagnosed after other causes of pleuritic chest pain are ruled out. It presents with tenderness on palpation over the area where the chest pain is reported.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman reports intermittent joint pains affecting her wrists, ankles and knees for the last six months. She describes each episode as involving pain, swelling and erythema in one of the above joints, which usually resolves with anti-inflammatory drugs over one to two days. Recently, the frequency of attacks has increased to two to three times per week from the previous two to three attacks every month. The last episode, involving the right knee, occurred three days ago. Examination in clinic was unremarkable for synovitis in any of the joints. Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial step?
options: Give the patient open access to the rheumatology clinic when they have the next attack
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Give the patient open access to the rheumatology clinic when they have the next attack

The patient is suffering from palindromic rheumatism, affecting mostly large joints. This is characterised by one or more features of inflammation, such as pain, swelling and erythema affecting an articular or periarticular site which lasts less than 72 hours before recovering completely. Any of the joints may be affected. In approximately 50% of patients, this may progress to rheumatoid arthritis (RA). The factors suggesting progression are small joint involvement, and a positive rheumatoid factor (RF) or anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP). The most common cause of recurrent or relapsing arthritis, however, is crystal arthritis. It is therefore important to ask the patient to report to clinic in the event of a future attack for synovial fluid aspiration and examination for urate and calcium pyrophosphate dehydrate (CPPD) crystals. Hyperuricaemia may be present but is not diagnostic and so testing for serum uric acid is not the correct answer here.

B X-ray of hands

This lady has a 6-month history and therefore X-rays are unlikely to be abnormal. An ultrasound (or MRI) to look for subclinical synovitis would be far more helpful than X-rays.

C Bone scan

Other diseases, such as systemic autoinflammatory disorders (periodic fever syndromes), Whipple’s disease, arthritis associated with hyperlipidaemia and intermittent hydrarthrosis, should be taken into account in the differential diagnosis of patients with recurrent arthritis. A bone scan would confer a lot of radiation for this young woman which is not justified by her symptoms.

D Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) testing

An ANA test is non-specific and unlikely to be helpful if positive. A far more useful test would be an anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP) antibody, which is more sensitive and more specific for a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) than rheumatoid factor, and can predate the clinical onset of RA.

E Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) testing

This presentation does not sound like vasculitis at all, and therefore ANCA testing is incorrect.

questions.question:
A 16-year-old boy presents with arthritis affecting his wrists, knees, ankles and some of his finger joints. He also has marked morning stiffness and a rash which affects his trunk and extremities. You understand from his mother that he has little interest in sport. You also notice a pericardial rub.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)102 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)5.6 × 10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)145 × 10⁹/L150 - 400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.0 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)100 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)58 mm/h1 - 20 mm/h
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)79 fL80 - 100 fL
ANA+ at 1:160
MRI of both knees is suggestive of synovitis; echocardiogram is suggestive of pericarditis.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

The ANA is positive in SLE but also may be present in oligoarticular and RF positive polyarticular JIA. Both SLE and systemic-onset JIA may manifest as fever and serositis, but the skin findings are different. In addition, malar rash, nephritis, cytopenia, hypocomplementaemia and anti-double-stranded DNA and other autoantibodies are seen only in SLE.

B Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

Whilst juvenile idiopathic arthritis (Still’s disease) normally occurs in younger children, it may occasionally present in adolescents or young adults. Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and rheumatoid factor (RF) are almost always negative in sJIA. Their presence should prompt consideration of alternative diagnoses. A positive RF, for example, may be associated with RF-positive polyarticular JIA, Sjögren's syndrome, or the early onset of adult- type rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in teenagers (although these disorders are not associated with high fevers and other sJIA features). Both RF and ANA may be present in children with mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD). However, these conditions rarely mimic sJIA. False-positive results may be seen in some patients. Some chronic infectious processes, such as subacute bacterial endocarditis, can cause unexplained fevers and a positive RF. A microcytic anaemia, which tends to be resistant to iron replacement and pericarditis, is often found. Patients may also present with symptoms consistent with uveitis. Options for pharmacotherapy include NSAIDs, corticosteroids, methotrexate and anti-TNF biologicals. A diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis is reserved for adult patients, whereas this patient is an adolescent.

C Rheumatoid arthritis

Multi-system rheumatologic disease may be distinguished from juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) by clinical features and laboratory findings. SLE often presents in adolescence with fever, rash and non-erosive arthritis.

D Sarcoidosis

Most of the reported cases of childhood sarcoidosis are accompanied by non-specific constitutional symptoms, such as fever, fatigue, malaise and weight loss, as well as symptoms from particular organs, such as the lungs, eyes, skin and lymph nodes. The joints tend not to be affected in children.

E Kawasaki disease

Kawasaki syndrome is a vasculitis in children, with prominent features including cervical lymphadenopathy and ‘strawberry red’ lips, palms and soles of feet. In some children coronary artery aneurysms may form.

questions.question:
A 61-year-old man who has a long history of rheumatoid arthritis, currently treated with methotrexate, presents to the Emergency Department with an acute arthritis affecting his right elbow. He tells you he was pruning roses a few days earlier in the garden and wonders whether something may have got into the joint. His rheumatoid disease has been stable for some time on methotrexate, and he takes lisinopril in addition for hypertension. His BP is 142/72 mmHg, pulse is 90/min and regular and he is pyrexial (38.6 °C). The elbow is erythematous and hot, there is a significant effusion and he is holding the joint in flexion because of pain on minimal movement.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)111 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)15.4 × 10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)203 × 10⁹/L150 - 400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)115 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)205 mg/L< 10 mg/L
X-ray elbowChanges consistent with rheumatoid arthritis

Which of the following is the most important next step?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Aspiration of joint

This patient has septic arthritis until proven otherwise. As such, it is essential that the diagnosis and likely pathogen are confirmed by joint aspiration.

B IV Flucloxacillin

Blind antibiotic use in a patient taking immunosuppression is ill advised. The joint should be aspirated and then broad-spectrum antibiotics started, pending sensitivities.

C Serum urate testing

Serum urate may be elevated, but it would not divert you from joint aspiration to rule out septic arthritis.

D Oral naproxen

Of course this patient needs analgesia, but the most important part of management is to aspirate the joint for a diagnosis.

E IV Co-amoxiclav

After joint aspiration, broad-spectrum antibiotics (usually benzylpenicillin and flucloxacillin) are started to cover joint sepsis.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man attends for review. He has evidence of arthritis affecting the shoulder, elbow, radiocarpal and knee joints bilaterally, with pain also in the left first metatarsophalangeal joint. An X-ray of the knee is shown below. Aspiration of the left knee reveals calcium pyrophosphate crystals. Serum uric acid level is slightly above the upper limit of normal. Other medical history of note is ulcerative colitis. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Gout

Gout is caused by monosodium urate crystals, which are fine, needle-like and negatively birefringent under polarised light.

B Pseudogout

The clinical picture of joint involvement, coupled with X-ray evidence of chondrocalcinosis and synovial fluid pyrophosphate crystals, is strongly suggestive of a diagnosis of pseudogout. The slightly elevated uric acid level and a history of ulcerative colitis are ‘red herrings’ in this case. Chondrocalcinosis is the deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals within the hyaline and fibrous cartilage. On X-ray, this is seen as a calcific appearance within the joint line (as shown above). Management involves use of simple painkillers and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents, coupled with physiotherapy where appropriate. Associated conditions include haemochromatosis and Wilson’s disease where there are other symptoms and signs, and it may be worth screening for these concomitant illnesses. Pseudogout has an equal male : female ratio, with the frequency increasing with advancing age; it is said to affect around 5% of subjects above the age of 30 years.

C Primary osteoarthritis

Osteoarthritis has a predilection for the knees, hips, interphalangeal joints, first carpometacarpal joints, first metatarsophalangeal joints and apophyseal (facet) joints of the lower cervical and lower lumbar spine. It is not associated with calcium pyrophosphate crystals.

D Rheumatoid arthritis

There is no suggestion of morning stiffness in this case history, and the distribution of affected joints and presence of calcium pyrophosphate crystals make rheumatoid arthritis unlikely.

E Septic arthritis

Acute monoarticular gout can be indistinguishable from septic arthritis in the history and clinical examination, and in some cases, these coexist. However, the identification of calcium pyrophosphate crystals and no mention of inflammatory cells in the synovial fluid make this answer incorrect.

questions.question: A 41-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner (GP), complaining of dry eyes, dry mouth and vaginal dryness on sexual intercourse. There is no significant past medical history; specifically, there is no history of rheumatoid arthritis or connective tissue disease. Which of the following is a likely clinical feature in this case?
options: 4 mm wetting per 5 minutes on Schirmer’s testing
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A 4 mm wetting per 5 minutes on Schirmer’s testing

The answer is 4 mm wetting per 5 minutes on Schirmer’s testing (Option A). This woman has Sjögren syndrome, as evidenced by her symptoms of dry mouth and dry eyes and the fact that other mucosal surfaces are affected. It may be primary or secondary (related to other autoimmune conditions). There is plasma cell infiltration of salivary and lacrimal glands with positive anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies, and a definitive positive Schirmer’s test is defined as <5 mm wetting per 5 minutes. Treatment involves use of artificial tears and screening for ophthalmic (corneal dryness and ulceration) and dental (caries) complications. Negative anti-Ro antibodies (Option C) is incorrect.

B Hypersalivation

Hypersalivation (Option B) is incorrect. This lady with Sjögren is likely to have decreased (not increased) parotid salivary gland flow. Increased salivation is a common problem secondary to antipsychotic medications such as clozapine. In such patients, glycopyrrolate can be useful, as it is an anticholinergic which does not cross the blood–brain barrier. Negative antinuclear antibodies (ANA) (Option D) is incorrect. This lady with Sjögren may have a positive ANA. ANA occurs in SLE (98%), scleroderma (95%), mixed connective tissue disease (100%), drug-induced lupus erythematosus (95%), Sjögren (60%), rheumatoid arthritis (45%), Raynaud’s phenomenon (40%) and polymyositis/dermatomyositis (35%). It can also occur in organ-specific autoimmune conditions such as autoimmune hepatitis (70%), primary biliary cholangitis (70%), Hashimoto’s (50%) and Grave’s disease (50%).

C Negative anti-Ro antibodies

This woman with Sjögren may have anti-Ro (or anti-La) antibodies. Anti-Ro antibodies have been detected in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) (32%), Sjögren syndrome (59%), idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (19%), systemic sclerosis (21%) and mixed connective tissue disease (29%).

D Negative antinuclear antibodies (ANA)

Low oestrogen levels (Option E) is incorrect.

E Low oestrogen levels

Her oestrogen levels are likely to be normal. She has dyspareunia because of Sjögren exocrinopathy, not related to her oestrogen levels. Oestrogen levels can become chronically low in post-menopausal women, primary ovarian pathology or suppression of the hypothalamus–pituitary–gonadal axis. In patients symptomatic of low oestrogen, hormone replacement therapy is an option.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology Clinic following a referral from his Dentist. She had been seeing the Hygienist after experiencing recurrent mouth ulcers. She has a past medical history of uveitis, after presenting with pain and redness of the eye and irritable bowel syndrome and was seen in the Sexual Health Clinic six months ago with vulval ulceration. Examination reveals multiple shallow ulcers in the mouth but no cutaneous lesions elsewhere. Cardiorespiratory examination is normal.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)122 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.2 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)219 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Creatinine71 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate32 mm/hour< 29 mm/hour

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Behçet syndrome

Behçet’s syndrome is a rare multisystem disease which classically presents with recurrent oral aphthous ulceration alongside systemic features. These include other cutaneous ulcers, genital ulcers, ocular symptoms (usually uveitis), GI symptoms, arthritis and nervous system disease. It is felt to be an autoimmune-driven vasculitis and is more common in East Asia and the Mediterranean. Patients usually present in early adulthood.

B HIV infection

HIV infection can result in ulceration in the oral cavity and genital region. Where it causes uveitis, it more commonly does so in the posterior, rather than the anterior, segment, as with this patient. Therefore, it is less likely to present with the features noted in this case but should, of course, be considered and tested for.

C Herpes simplex

Herpes simplex may refer to either type 1 or type 2. Type 1 classically causes oral ulcers, whereas type 2 causes genital herpes. Type 1 can additionally result in ocular disease, but it would be unusual for the ulceration to occur in both regions and in eye disease, all disseminated in time.

D Crohn’s disease

Crohn’s disease can result in oral ulceration and symptoms outside the GI tract, including uveitis, although the combination of oral and genital ulceration is more suspicious of Behçet’s syndrome.

E Reactive arthritis

Reactive arthritis occurs after enteric or genitourinary infections. Neither appears to have occurred here. Additionally, ocular symptoms tend to be conjunctivitis and arthritis is absent.

questions.question: A 69-year-old woman attends the Rheumatology Clinic with progressive right knee pain affecting her ability to walk to the shops. The pain is constant throughout the day and is worsened by movement and weight-bearing. She denies fever and has been well with no recent illnesses. Her past medical history includes hypertension and type II diabetes. On examination, her temperature is 36.1 °C. She has a heart rate of 77 bpm, with a blood pressure of 146/92 mmHg. On auscultation, her heart sounds are normal and vesicular chest sounds are heard throughout, with oxygen saturations of 97% on room air. Her right knee is mildly swollen and tender to touch; it feels warm but is not erythematous. There is palpable crepitus on movement and a small prepatellar effusion is noted. Heberden’s and Bouchard’s nodes are seen. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Colchicine

Colchicine is used in the treatment of gout. Gout is a crystal arthropathy associated with hyperuricaemia secondary to chronic kidney disease, a purine-rich diet or drug therapy, including thiazide diuretics. Gout presents as an acutely painful joint, typically in the first metatarsophalangeal joint. It is uncommon for gout to present as progressive knee degeneration and gout does not account for this patient’s Heberden’s and Bouchard’s nodes.

B Intra-articular corticosteroids

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend that intra-articular corticosteroid injections be considered as an adjunct to treatment for osteoarthritis, but it should not be the mainstay of treatment. First-line agents such as paracetamol and topical ibuprofen should be tried first.

C Oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs

If oral paracetamol and topical NSAIDs fail to treat the pain associated with OA, oral NSAIDs, such as ibuprofen, can be trialled, provided there are no contraindications.

D Paracetamol and topical ibuprofen

This patient has osteoarthritis (OA), a degenerative arthritis capable of affecting multiple joints. OA of weight- bearing joints such as the hips and knees is very common. In OA, bony swellings at the distal interphalangeal joints (Heberden’s nodes) and proximal interphalangeal joints (Bouchard’s nodes) are often seen, as described in this question. Unlike inflammatory arthritis, OA does not have a typical pattern of early morning joint stiffness that improves throughout the day and pain is often constant and worsened with movement. Restricted movement, joint effusions and crepitus are all signs of OA. The first-line treatment for OA is oral paracetamol and topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as topical ibuprofen.

E Prednisolone and methotrexate

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend that intra-articular corticosteroid injections be considered as an adjunct to treatment for osteoarthritis, but it should not be the mainstay of treatment. First-line agents such as paracetamol and topical ibuprofen should be tried first.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with three weeks history of daily fevers, an erythematous rash which appears to get worse with the spikes of fever, joint pains affecting both knees, his right elbow and his left ankle, and extreme fatigue. He is unable to hold down his job as a builder because of these symptoms. On examination, his temperature is 37.3°C, heart rate is 68/min and regular. There is a pericardial rub, the chest is clear. You confirm evidence of oligoarthritis.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)119 g/L135–175 g/L
White Cell Count (WCC)12.8 × 10⁹/L4–11 × 109/l
Platelets (PLT)149 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 109/l
Sodium(Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine95 micromol/l50–120 µmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)75 mm/1 hour0–10 mm/ 1st hour
CRP210 mg/L0–10 mg/L
Ferritin590 microg/L20–250 µg/L

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Adult onset Juvenile Chronic Arthritis

The answer is Adult onset juvenile chronic arthritis (JCA) - The fevers lasting for more than 2 weeks, coupled with oligoarthritis, an erythematous rash and pericarditis fits with systemic JCA. The fever seen with JCA exhibits periodicity, and occurs once or twice per day. Autoantibodies are generally unhelpful, with ANA and rheumatoid factor positivity being seen in approximately 10% of patients. NSAIDs form the basis of symptom relief, and a short course of systemic corticosteroids can be considered to gain disease control. Second-line agents include both methotrexate and anti-TNF based therapies.

B Haemochromatosis

Haemochromatosis is incorrect, because although the ferritin is elevated, this is because ferritin is an acute phase protein, rather than representing iron overload.

C Rheumatoid arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect, it is usually associated with a symmetrical small joint polyarthritis, and is therefore unlikely here.

D Septic arthritis

Septic arthritis is incorrect, it is a possible differential for the oligoarthritis seen here, but is less likely given the 3 week history of fevers, suggesting a subacute presentation.

E Seronegative arthritis

Seronegative arthritis, is incorrect, it is often associated with lower back pain / sacroilitis, or enthesopathies such as plantar fasciitis. None of those features are seen here.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old Asian woman was referred to the Rheumatology Clinic with long-standing joint problems. She described initial involvement of the small joints of the hands, which resolved after a few weeks. Now the main joints involved are the wrists, elbows and knees. Before she migrated to the UK from Pakistan 2 years ago, she had suffered recurrent ear infections and a few episodes of nasal septum inflammation. On each episode, she was treated with antibiotics and analgesia. She has a family history of systemic lupus erythematosus and she is on amlodipine for hypertension. On examination, the wrists and the knees are swollen and tender with reduced active and passive movement. The nose is saddle-shaped and the right upper ear cartilage is red and tender.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)95 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.0 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)86 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour
Sodium (Na⁺)146 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.8 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea4.6 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)120 μmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Rheumatoid factor (RF)Negative
Antinuclear antibody (ANA)Negative
Urine dipstickNegative

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)

This lady has outer ear inflammation, ie of the cartilaginous pinna, and relapsing arthritis which are key differentiators from GPA. Although we are not given an ANCA result (expecting a cANCA with GPA), the renal function is normal and urine dipstick is inactive.

B Relapsing polychondritis

This lady has inflammation of the outer ear, nasal septum and relapsing remitting arthralgia/arthritis consistent with relapsing polychondritis. Relapsing polychondritis is a disorder that affects, cartilaginous and connective tissues causing episodic inflammation and destruction. Onset is typically in middle age and it occurs in equal frequency in men and women. The most common symptom is inflammation of the external ear and nasal cartilage. It is often associated with arthritis involving both small and large joints. Characteristic of the disease are bouts of inflammation that heal over weeks. Recurrent inflammation results in destruction of cartilaginous tissue resulting in floppy ears and a saddle nose. Biopsy of affected cartilaginous tissue will confirm the diagnosis.

C Mixed connective tissue disorder

The ANA is negative and she has no features of connective tissue disease.

D Systemic sclerosis

In systemic sclerosis, ear and nose involvement is not common and Raynaud’s is almost universal.

E Polymyalgia rheumatica

The lady has a negative ANA.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old woman presents to the Respiratory Clinic with increased shortness of breath. She has suffered from Raynaud’s syndrome for some time, and around 6–9 months ago began treatment for gastro-oesophageal reflux. Other past history of note includes smoking of 10 cigarettes per day. On examination, her blood pressure is 152/92 mmHg, with a pulse of 83 bpm. Auscultation of the chest reveals fine inspiratory crackles throughout both lung fields.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)109 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)5.9 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)135 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)141 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)142 μmol/L50–120 µmol/L
FEV2.1
FVC2.3
Adjusted KCOLow

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Asthma

Polyphonic wheezes are more likely to be heard, as crackles may signify infection.

B Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)

An obstructive spirometry pattern would be found and the extrapulmonary features are not associated with COPD.

C Systemic sclerosis

The constellation of symptoms and signs seen here, with Raynaud’s, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, dyspnoea and a restrictive pattern of spirometry, is highly suggestive of systemic sclerosis with pulmonary fibrosis. Antinuclear antibody testing is usually positive, high-resolution CT scanning reveals changes characteristic of interstitial lung disease: pulmonary fibrosis. Calcium channel blockers, prostaglandins and cyclophosphamide have all been used in the treatment of systemic sclerosis related lung disease, and PDE-5 inhibitors are now used extensively for control of pulmonary hypertension. One would expect an obstructive pattern of spirometry, and onset of asthma at this age would be unusual.

D Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

Although the features could be consistent with SLE, the absence of any rashes or cytopaenias make SLE less likely than systemic sclerosis.

E Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

The most striking feature dissuading you from the diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is Raynaud’s phenomenon, which is strongly linked to connective tissue disease.

questions.question: A 56-year-old woman who suffered a road traffic accident some years ago presents to the clinic for review. She has been complaining of increasing pain and weakness in her right arm over the past few months and is now unable to work. Past history of note includes osteoarthritis. On examination, there is weakness and wasting of the triceps, wrist and finger extensors, loss of the triceps jerk and sensory loss over the middle fingers of the hand. Prolapse of which intervertebral disc is most likely to be responsible for her symptoms and signs?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A C4–5

C4–5 (C5 nerve root): A herniation at this level can cause shoulder pain and weakness in the deltoid muscle at the top of the upper arm, and does not usually cause numbness or tingling.

B C5–6

C5–6 (C6 nerve root): A C5–6 disc herniation can cause weakness of the biceps (muscles in the front of the upper arms) and wrist extensor muscles. Numbness and tingling along with pain can radiate to the thumb side of the hand. This is one of the most common levels for a cervical disc herniation to occur. C7–T1 (C8 nerve root): This level is located at the very bottom of the neck, where the cervical spine meets the thoracic, or upper, back. A herniation here can cause weakness with handgrip, along with numbness and tingling and pain that radiates down the arm to the little finger side of hand. T1–2 disc protrusion specifically refers to the deterioration of one or more of the intervertebral discs in the thoracic (middle) segment of the spine. The protrusion of a disc between any of the 12 vertebrae in the thoracic spine (T1–12) can cause severe pain and other symptoms if nerve compression is present. Disc protrusion in the thoracic spine, however, is somewhat rare because the thoracic spinal segment is attached directly to the ribcage, keeping the 12 thoracic vertebrae relatively stable and stationary. Lumbar disc protrusion (in the lower back) and cervical disc protrusion (in the neck) are much more common.

C C6–7

A lateral cervical disc protrusion at the C6–7 level (i.e. the disc between the 6th and 7th cervical vertebrae) compresses the exiting C7 nerve and thus causes pain and weakness over the C7 myotome (triceps, wrist and finger extensors), loss of the triceps jerk and loss of sensation over the C7 dermatome. Pain relief and immobilisation may be appropriate for initial management, although in those who fail to respond, MRI and assessment for surgical decompression are recommended.

D C7–T1

The cervical spine is constructed around the vertebrae, or the seven stacked bony building blocks in the spine.

E T1–2

They are numbered from top to bottom as C1 to C7. The nerve that is affected by the cervical disc herniation is the one exiting the spine at that level, so at the C5–6 level it is the C6 nerve root that is affected.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. Over the past few months, she has developed a photosensitive rash, which is particularly prominent on her face, and small joint polyarthritis which is affecting her job as a data operator. You note evidence of active arthritis affecting her fingers, wrists, both elbows, and her feet. Urine is positive for both blood and protein. A picture of her face is shown below. Which of the following is most likely to be positive?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Anti-CCP

Anti-CCP antibodies are a marker of disease activity in rheumatoid arthritis. Although that may be a reasonable alternative diagnosis, the facial rash is a stronger pointer towards systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) here.

B Anti-nuclear antibody

The rash seen here is suggestive of the erythematous changes seen in patients with active SLE, as is the evidence of arthritis and renal vasculitis. Anti-nuclear antibody testing has a sensitivity of 95% for SLE, but the titre is not closely related to disease activity. As such, other measures, such as complement testing, are more useful in assessing this.

C Anti-Scl 70

Scl 70 positivity is a marker of diffuse systemic sclerosis, which is not suggested here because of the absence of other features such as sclerodactyly and peripheral calcinosis.

D c-ANCA

c-ANCA positivity is most associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis, in which pulmonary and renal vasculitis is seen, often with evidence of chronic sinusitis. There is no evidence of pulmonary vasculitis here.

E p-ANCA

p-ANCA positivity is seen in around half of patients with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which is usually associated with symptoms of poorly controlled asthma. It is also seen in patients suffering from primary sclerosing cholangitis.

questions.question: A 76-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner with progressively worsening joint pain and mobility. She is struggling to get dressed in the morning and to achieve small tasks such as carrying a cup of tea. The pain is constant throughout the day, although it improves with rest and paracetamol. Her past medical history includes hypothyroidism, for which she takes levothyroxine 75 micrograms once daily. On examination, her observations are recorded within normal limits. On auscultation, chest sounds are clear and heart sounds are normal. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender. She has crepitus over the hip and knee joints. There is a visible deformity to her proximal (PIPJs) and distal interphalangeal joints (DIPJs) (shown below). There are no skin or nail changes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Gout

Gout is a crystal arthropathy associated with hyperuricaemia. Causes of hyperuricaemia include chronic kidney disease, a purine-rich diet and drug therapy, including thiazide diuretics. Gout presents as an acutely painful joint, typically in the first metatarsal joint. Men are more commonly affected than women. The clinical history does not suggest that this patient has hyperuricaemia and the pattern of joint involvement does not reflect gout, making it an incorrect answer.

B Osteoarthritis (OA)

OA is a degenerative arthritis affecting multiple joints. The pathological basis of the disease is characterised by loss of cartilage and significant articular and periarticular inflammation. No single cause has been identified, but risk factors for OA include obesity, trauma, repetitive injury (eg in extreme sport) and certain diseases leading to secondary OA such as pre-existing joint disease and metabolic disease (eg haemochromatosis). Symptoms of OA include joint pain with clear functional limitation. Unlike inflammatory arthritis, OA does not have a typical pattern of early morning joint stiffness that improves throughout the day. Restricted movement, joint effusions and crepitus are all signs of OA. OA of weight-bearing joints such as the hips and knees, as well as OA of the hands, are common. DIPJs are more often involved than PIPJs. This photograph shows a patient with bony swellings at the DIPJs (Heberden’s nodes) and PIPJs (Bouchard’s nodes), which are commonly seen in OA.

C Psoriatic arthritis

Image source: https://dermnetnz.org/topics/heberden-bouchard-nodes/ Psoriatic arthritis belongs to a group of spondyloarthropathies associated with the HLA-B27 antigen. Skin changes may or may not be seen. A common pattern of joint disease is distal interphalangeal arthritis with adjacent nail dystrophy. In approximately 5% of patients with psoriatic arthritis, severe deformity, known as arthritis mutilans, secondary to severe periarticular osteolysis and bone shortening may occur. The pattern of joint disease in this patient, combined with the clinical history, is more suggestive of OA.

D Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a symmetrical, polyarticular inflammatory arthritis associated with synovial inflammation. It is more common in women. Early morning stiffness is a common complaint, with joint pain and stiffness improving throughout the day. Hand disease in RA commonly involves the metacarpophalangeal joints (MCPJs), causing a subluxation deformity referred to as ulnar deviation. RA of the PIPJs can cause fixed flexion deformities (Boutonnière deformity) or fixed hyperextension (swan neck deformity). These are not the changes seen in this patient. That, combined with the clinical history of progressive pain that fails to improve throughout the day, is more suggestive of osteoarthritis.

E Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an inflammatory autoimmune disorder affecting multiple organ systems, including the cardiovascular, renal and nervous systems. The disease commonly involves the skin and joints, causing arthralgia and distinctive rashes such as the ‘butterfly rash’ across the face. Although it is more common in women, SLE is usually diagnosed between 20 and 40 years of age. It is less likely for this patient to be presenting with her first symptoms of SLE at 76 years of age.

questions.question: A 26-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of feeling lethargic and feverish with a loss of appetite. He also reports aching joints starting with his upper limbs and now affecting his lower limbs, particularly his left knee, which he reports to have become very tender and swollen in the last 24 hours. There is no history of trauma, and he has no past medical history of note. However, he did visit his General Practitioner earlier in the week due to experiencing burning on micturition. On examination, his left knee is erythematous, swollen and warm to the touch. He is reluctant to extend his knee due to pain. There are multiple vesicular lesions over these extremities which he reports to be new. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Ceftriaxone

This patient likely has disseminated gonococcal arthritis, given the history of polyarthritis and acute-onset knee pain, swelling and erythema. It is not uncommon for patients with gonococcal arthritis to experience extra- articular features such as urethritis, tenosynovitis and cutaneous symptoms, including a papular or vesicular rash, most commonly on the extremities. The history of burning on micturition is suggestive of underlying urethritis in this scenario. Disseminated gonococcal arthritis is caused by the Gram-negative organism Neisseria gonorrhoeae for which the treatment is intravenous ceftriaxone.

B Colchicine

Colchicine is used in the treatment of gout and Behçet syndrome. Key features of Behçet syndrome include oral and genital ulceration, uveitis and musculoskeletal involvement. Meanwhile, gout presents with acute-onset inflammation of a joint (mostly the first metatarsal joint) with risk factors including male sex, age over 40 years and dietary habits including high red meat, seafood and alcohol intake. Neither of these conditions matches the presentation of this patient, making colchicine a less appropriate management option.

C Flucloxacillin

Flucloxacillin is used in the treatment of non-gonococcal septic arthritis. Non-gonococcal arthritis is more common in the elderly population, particularly those with co-existing joint disease or prosthetic joints. Men are more likely to be affected than women and the causative organisms also differ with the most common being Staphylococcus aureus, followed by streptococcal species and Staphylococcus epidermidis. Given the young age, history of dysuria, and a vesicular rash gonococcal arthritis secondary to N. gonorrhoeae should be expected.

D Naproxen

Naproxen and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are the first line of choice for osteoarthritis and reactive arthritis. Reactive arthritis is a sterile synovitis triggered by an infectious agent outside of the joint. The most common examples include sexually transmitted diseases, particularly Chlamydia trachomatis and dysenteric infections such as Salmonella, Shigella, Clostridium and Yersinia species. However, the systemic upset, along with the history of polyarthritis, vesicular rash and dysuria make gonococcal arthritis the more likely diagnosis.

E Prednisolone

Prednisolone is used in the treatment of inflammatory arthritis, including rheumatoid arthritis. However, it is uncommon for inflammatory arthropathies to cause fever, reduced appetite and dysuria, and these symptoms suggest an underlying infective cause.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with chest pain to the Emergency Department. She smokes approximately 30 cigarettes per day. There is no history of hypersensitivity to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents. There is pain with coughing and deep breathing, with tenderness of the 2 to 5 costochondral junctions with the sternum. Chest X-ray is unremarkable and electrocardiogram (ECG) shows no acute changes; saturations are 98% on air. Which of the following would be the most appropriate intervention in this case?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Low-molecular weight heparin

nd th

B Aspirin 75 mg po

A pulmonary embolism is very unlikely given the normal ECG, lack of tachycardia, normal oxygen saturations on room air and tenderness on palpation of the chest wall. Aspirin 75 mg would be inadequate to treat acute coronary syndrome, which is unlikely in any case given her lack of ECG changes and no mention of cardiac enzymes being elevated.

C Naproxen 250 mg qds

This patient has costochondritis (Tietze syndrome), which has a higher prevalence in women and is commoner over the age of 40 years. It is associated with tenderness over the costochondral junctions and/or sternum, pain on coughing and deep breathing, and equal involvement with both sides of the chest. Non-steroidals would be an appropriate first-line intervention for pain relief. It is of course an ideal opportunity to reinforce advice about smoking cessation.

D Amoxicillin 500 mg po tds

This lady does not have productive cough, fever, raised CRP or crackles on examination, and therefore antibiotics in this case are inappropriate and may perpetuate antibiotic resistance.

E Fluticasone 50 μg inhaler bd

There is no suggestion that this is an exacerbation of asthma – she has no wheeze or dyspnoea, but does have pain on palpation of her chest wall at the costochondral junction.

questions.question: A 67-year-old man, who has previously been given a diagnosis of osteoarthritis, presents to the Acute Medical Assessment Unit with pain in his first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint. He has a past history of hypertension, for which he takes bendroflumethiazide 5 mg/day. On examination, the joint is hot and red and has a knobbly appearance. The X-ray is shown below: By Hellerhoff [CC BY-SA 3.0 (https://creativecommons.org/Licenses/by-sa/3.0)], from Wikimedia Commons Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management for this patient?
options: Stop bendroflumethiazide and substitute a calcium antagonist
Advise dietary restriction of rich foods
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Start allopurinol

This patient has chronic tophaceous gout. If a patient is already receiving urate-lowering therapy, then there is no value in suspending it during an acute flare, and subsequent reintroduction may precipitate an attack. In the absence of any urate-lowering attack, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend the use of xanthine-oxidase inhibitors, such as allopurinol or febuxostat, first line. Uricosuric drugs, such as sulfinpyrazone or benzbromarone, can be used second line where prescribed by a specialist.

B Start ibuprofen

Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are beneficial as a short-term therapy in flares but should not be continued long-term due to their implication on renal function.

C Stop bendroflumethiazide and substitute a calcium antagonist

The X-ray shows erosive changes in the first MTP joint, with well-maintained joint space and coexisting soft tissue swelling. This, along with the presentation, demonstrates that the patient has chronic tophaceous gout, which is usually associated with chronic renal impairment and long-term use of diuretic therapy. Deposits of sodium urate occur in the skin and around joints; larger deposits are unsightly and may ulcerate. Diuretics should be substituted for another medication where the condition is associated with diuretic use.

D Start fLucloxacillin

The description and radiological findings are not consistent with septic arthritis, and flucloxacillin is not an appropriate empirical antibiotic for this indication.

E Advise dietary restriction of rich foods

The NICE guidelines recommend eating a healthy, balanced diet rather than following any specific diet. There is not enough evidence that specific diets sufficiently lower urate levels.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with a long-standing history of type II diabetes returns to the Foot Clinic for review one week after beginning co-amoxiclav for an ulcer on his left heel. He and the chiropodists feel that it is not improving significantly. Examination reveals a 2-cm diameter lesion affecting the left heel. There is fresh pus and exudate around the edge of the lesion, and your probe easily reaches the bone. C-reactive protein (CRP) is still elevated at 170 mg/L (185 at presentation). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Add rifampicin

Adding rifampicin may be useful in the event of deep-seated staphylococcal infection, although it will not achieve clearance in the event there is significant osteomyelitis, and this must be ruled out first. Although clindamycin achieves very good tissue penetration and has good activity against staphylococcal infection, it is most important to rule out osteomyelitis, which may require surgical resection first.

B Add clindamycin

This is the least appropriate option here. It is clear that infection is not improving with co-amoxiclav, and both investigation for osteomyelitis and a change of antibiotic therapy are likely to be required.

C Admit for intravenous (IV) vancomycin

Vancomycin IV is effective against staphylococcal infection. However, with the possibility of mixed infection here, coupled with possible osteomyelitis, MRI scanning is a more appropriate next step.

D Continue co-amoxiclav

While adding rifampicin, clindamycin and vancomycin could all be considered for deep-seated staphylococcal infection, they should only be considered as part of a treatment strategy which includes MRI and orthopaedic review. Continuing co-amoxiclav alone is not an option.

E Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)

Osteomyelitis is a possibility and should be excluded as soon as possible with MRI. In the event there is evidence of osteomyelitis, then surgical review for possible debridement is the most appropriate next step. At this point, further blind antibiotic therapy without imaging evidence is not advised.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of a painful right knee. He reports that he is now unable to bear weight on his knee due to pain despite taking regular paracetamol. During this time, he also complains of lethargy and reduced appetite. He has a past medical history of Crohn’s disease which is well-controlled with azathioprine. On examination, he has a temperature of 37.9 °C with a heart rate of 110 bpm and regular, with a BP of 105/65 mmHg. His right knee is swollen and erythematous with a fixed-flexion deformity. There is a papular rash over the extremities.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)145 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)14.5 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)255 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.2 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea6.1 mmol/L1.8–7.1 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)80 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate45 mm/h< 15 mm/h

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Behçet syndrome

Pseudogout is caused by calcium pyrophosphate deposition, causing an acute inflammatory arthritis. Many different joints can be affected by pseudogout, including the knees. Generally, pseudogout affects older people or those with certain metabolic conditions such as haemochromatosis or hyperparathyroidism. The presence of low-grade fever and systemic symptoms makes pseudogout very unlikely.

B Gout

Behçet syndrome is a chronic multisystem inflammatory disorder that classically presents as recurrent oral ulceration. The onset of symptoms is typically between the ages of 30 and 40 years with men and women being equally likely of developing the disease. Key features of Behçet syndrome include oral and genital ulceration, uveitis and musculoskeletal involvement. This does not completely fit with this patient’s presentation, making it unlikely here.

C Gonococcal arthritis

This patient likely has gonococcal arthritis given the history of acute-onset knee pain, swelling and erythema with low-grade fevers and raised inflammatory markers. A fixed-flexion deformity is highly suggestive of a septic joint, like in gonococcal arthritis. Furthermore, it is not uncommon for patients with gonococcal arthritis to experience extra-articular features such as urethritis, tenosynovitis and cutaneous symptoms, including a papular or vesicular rash, most commonly on the extremities. Gonococcal arthritis tends to affect young, healthy adults who are sexually active, and women are more frequently affected than men. Gout is caused by the deposition of urate crystals, causing attacks of acute inflammatory arthritis. The most affected joint is the first metatarsal, although the knee, ankle, wrist and hand can also be affected. Risk factors for gout include male sex, age over 40 years and dietary habits, including high red meat, seafood and alcohol intake. This patient is unlikely to have gout based on the lack of these features.

D Pseudogout

Reactive arthritis is a sterile synovitis triggered by an infectious agent outside of the joint. The most common examples include sexually transmitted disease, particularly Chlamydia trachomatis and dysenteric infections such as Salmonella, Shigella, Clostridium and Yersinia species. The post-sexually transmitted disease form is approximately ten times more common in men, while post-dysenteric disease affects men and women equally.

E Reactive arthritis

Not all infections will go on to produce reactive arthritis, but it is an important consideration to have when a person presents with acute joint pain, especially young and healthy adults. Features of reactive arthritis include arthritis, conjunctivitis and urethritis. Mucocutaneous symptoms include circinate balanitis (erythematous and ulcerative lesions on the glans penis), keratoderma blennorrhagia, and nail involvement is also seen, including thickening and onycholysis. It is uncommon for reactive arthritis to cause a systemic upset, as seen in this scenario, making gonococcal arthritis more likely to be the diagnosis.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old self-employed man presents with a 4-month history of progressive dyspnoea and fatigue. He complains of a painful rash on the backs of his hands. He also reports redness on the face and the central upper chest. The rash worsens after sun exposure. He has not noticed any blisters. On further questioning, he has noticed a significant weight loss with reduced appetite. He takes regular analgesics for migraines. He is allergic to penicillin. He is a non-smoker and drinks alcohol socially.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)100 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)8.0 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)490 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)40 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)30 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour
Liver enzymesNormal
Creatine kinase (CK)860 IU/L23–175 IU/L
Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA)+
Chest examinationUnremarkable
Abdomen examinationUnremarkable
Cranial nervesIntact
ToneNormal throughout
ReflexesIntact
Power5/5 except hip flexors 4/5
OtherDowngoing plantars bilaterally; no sensation deficits

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

Although ANA positivity and photosensitivity would fit with this, and SLE frequently involves the skin, the eruption in the photograph is very suggestive of dermatomyositis.

B Porphyria cutanea tarda

This is another photosensitive disorder, but it typically leads to blistering at sun-exposed sites. There is usually a history of chronic liver disease. ANA positivity and raised inflammatory markers would not be expected.

C Polymyalgia rheumatica

Violaceous ‘Gottron’s papules’ over the knuckles. Linear violaceous changes over the dorsal surfaces of the fingers. Nail-fold inflammation with dilated capillaries. The ‘shawl sign’ describes erythema over the upper back and posterior neck. Weakness of the major proximal muscle groups, although some patients will have skin involvement alone (‘amyopathic dermatomyositis’). Rarely, involuntary muscles may be involved, leading to potentially dangerous or even fatal difficulties in swallowing or breathing. Calcification can occur in juvenile dermatomyositis, but is uncommon in adults. Investigations should include creatine kinase, antinuclear antibody and skin biopsy; electromyography and/or muscle biopsy can confirm myositis. Screening for underlying neoplasia (such as CT chest, abdomen and pelvis) is generally advised in adult cases. This causes muscle pains and stiffness, but is not associated with rash.

D Guillain–Barré syndrome

This is a disorder of the peripheral nervous system which presents with weakness and paraesthesia, usually beginning in the legs. It usually follows an infection and is not associated with a rash.

E Dermatomyositis

Clues include the violaceous eruption and nail-fold inflammation seen in the image, history of photosensitivity, positive ANA and elevated CK. Dermatomyositis is a rare disease in which a characteristic rash is associated with myositis. When it develops over the age of 40 years, about one third of patients prove to have an underlying carcinoma. It is more common in females. Typical features include: A red or violaceous peri-orbital eruption known as the ‘heliotrope rash’; there may be associated oedema.

questions.question:
A 59-year-old man presents with an acute pain and effusion in his right knee. He is on haemodialysis for chronic kidney disease related to type 1 diabetes and takes a number of medications including vitamin D and cinacalcet. On examination, his blood pressure is 155/89 mmHg, his pulse is 80 bpm regular, his temperature is 37.6 °C. He does not appear to be fluid overloaded. He has psoriatic plaques on knees and elbows.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin104 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.7 × 10⁹/L4–11 × 10⁹/L
Platelets179 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Corrected Ca2.15 mmol/L2.20–2.60 mmol/L
Creatinine540 µmol/L (pre-dialysis)50–120 µmol/L
Knee effusionNeutrophils and rhomboid crystals identified, weakly positively birefringent

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Gout

Gouty crystals are needle shaped and negatively birefringent.

B Hydroxyapatite arthritis

Hydroxyapatite crystals are associated with a very destructive type of arthritis, usually in the shoulders of elderly women; heavily blood stained fluid is usually found.

C Pseudogout

This man has end-stage kidney disease and hyperparathyroidism, as evidenced by his cinacalcet prescription, and his low normal calcium. Hyperparathyroidism is associated with pseudogout (chondrocalcinosis) which may present acutely as an oligoarthritis, similar to gout, in shoulders, elbows or ankles or knees. Diagnosis is based on negative culture, and non- or weakly positively birefringent rhomboid or rod-shaped crystals. NSAIDs are used in patients without renal dysfunction, but may worsen salt and water retention and blood pressure in this patient, so colchicine may be a more appropriate choice.

D Psoriatic arthritis

Although this patient has psoriasis, the presence of crystals in the synovial fluid make a crystal arthritis far more likely.

E Osteoarthritis

The history is too acute for osteoarthritis and the synovial fluid findings crystalize the diagnosis of pseudogout.

questions.question: A 39-year-old man presents to Rheumatology Clinic after noticing a new swelling on the side of his finger. He has noticed that the swelling has been worsening over the past several months. He has a past medical history of rheumatoid arthritis (RA), hypertension and hyperlipidaemia. He normally takes methotrexate, paracetamol, ramipril, atorvastatin and aspirin. A photograph of his hand is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Xanthoma

There is some variety in presentation, but typically it is a small nodule which progressively grows, becomes necrotic and sloughs. The absence of such features makes this an unlikely diagnosis.

B Rheumatoid nodule

This patient has developed a rheumatoid nodule. These are firm swellings in subcutaneous tissue, often occurring over bony prominences, but also in the lungs. A quarter of patients with RA develop nodules which are usually asymptomatic. They consist of fibrous layers. Methotrexate can make nodules worse, while rituximab can make them better. Surgical removal is often successful. BCCs are slow growing and locally invasive epidermal tumours of the skin. They occur in sun-exposed areas. They are small and have a pearly or translucent appearance with telangiectasia. The absence of such features makes this an unlikely diagnosis. Xanthomas are flat, yellow plaques appearing in the 30s or 40s, typically in women. The lesions tend to become static and do not regress. They are associated with high cholesterol-rich beta-lipoproteins (LDLs). This nodule, however, is not flat and does not have the typical yellowish colour.

C Basal cell carcinoma (BCC)

SCCs are malignant tumours arising from keratinising cells of the epidermis and can be locally invasive and sometimes metastatic. Presentation is as an individual nodular keratinising or crusting lesion which can ulcerate.

D Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)

Keratoacanthomas are rapidly growing squamous lesions that appear over months and spontaneously resolve.

E Keratoacanthoma

They are solitary, round and skin coloured or reddish papules which may project like a horn. The absence of a centre keratin horn-like structure makes this unlikely.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old man is reviewed in the Rheumatology Clinic. He has suffered from arthritis for many years but is now finding it very difficult to manage at home, particularly with respect to cooking food and eating. His hands have become progressively more disfigured. He takes thyroxine 100 µg/day and amlodipine. He is otherwise well, a scar over his neck is noted.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)126 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)9.4 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)151 × 10⁹/L400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.7 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)112 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Corrected calcium (Ca²⁺)2.4 mmol/L2.2–2.7 mmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)30 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Hyperparathyroidism

Although hyperparathyroidism does result in the shortening of the distal phalanx, it is not associated with the more proximal deformity seen in this patient, and the blood tests are all in the normal range.

B Osteoarthritis

Osteoarthritis is associated with finger stiffness and the formation of Heberden’s and Bouchard’s nodes rather than bone resorption and deformity, which seem apparent here.

C Pseudohypoparathyroidism

Pseudohypoparathyroidism is associated with the shortening of the fifth metacarpal and hypocalcaemia, rather than the picture of arthritis mutilans seen here.

D Psoriatic arthritis

This patient has long-standing arthritis with arthritis mutilans. Shortening, particularly of the distal interphalangeal joints, is consistent with psoriatic arthritis. It is likely that this patient’s active disease burnt out some time ago, given that the routine blood tests are in the normal range.

E Rheumatoid arthritis

Rheumatoid arthritis is associated with arthritis mutilans in advanced diseases. However, the predominantly distal features of this patient’s disease count against rheumatoid arthritis, as opposed to psoriatic arthritis, as the cause in this patient.

questions.question:
A 15-year-old boy presents with a 4-month history of fever, lethargy and a generalised macular rash, which comes and goes. Before the episode, he was well. He had no previous medical history or recent illness and there was no recent travel abroad. On examination, temperature was 38.5 °C, blood pressure 125/75 mmHg, pulse of 100 bpm. The chest was clear and there were no heart murmurs on auscultation. A widespread non-blanching macular rash is seen over the chest and abdomen. There is swelling of the interphalangeal joints of both hands and feet with slight tenderness. Lymph nodes are palpable on the supraclavicular, axillary and inguinal regions. Examination of the abdomen also reveals a palpable mass on both right and left hypochondrium.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)135 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)14.0 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)380 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)145 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.8 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)89 μmol/L50–120 μmol/L
Rheumatoid factor (RF)Negative
Antinuclear antibody (ANA)Negative
Anti-dsDNANegative
Anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titreNot detected
Electrocardiogram (ECG)Sinus rhythm

What is the most likely underlying diagnosis from the choices listed below?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Acute rheumatic fever

The history is too long, the ASO titre is negative and there are no features of carditis with a normal ECG and PR interval.

B Juvenile systemic lupus erythematosus

The antinuclear antibody is negative and there are significant systemic features (high fevers).

C Pauciarticular Still’s disease

In pauciarticular Still’s disease, antinuclear antibodies are present. Large joints are affected and most patients develop classic features of seronegative spondyloarthritis.

D Reactive arthritis

The history is too long, there is no infective precipitant and the generalised lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly does not fit with reactive arthritis.

E Systemic Still’s disease

Systemic Still’s disease and other forms of juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA) usually begin before the age of 16 years. There are different types of JRA with different presenting features. Systemic Still’s is characterised by systemic features, high fever, rashes, generalised lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly with minor features of arthritis. Systemic features may precede the onset of arthritis. Rheumatoid factor and antinuclear antibodies are absent.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents the Acute Medical Unit with an acutely swollen and sore left knee. She and several family members who attended a family BBQ experienced acute-onset abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea that lasted several days, just one week previously. She also reports a gritty sensation in her eyes. Examination reveals a swollen left knee which is warm to touch but maintaining a good range of motion. Synovial fluid examination is sterile, with a raised neutrophil count. Her knee pain is uncontrolled despite the maximum dose of naproxen. What is the next most appropriate management for the knee symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Intra-articular steroid injection

The question describes a combination of oligoarthritis with a sterile aspirate and likely conjunctivitis following GI symptoms. The most likely diagnosis is reactive arthritis, probably following Campylobacter jejuni infection acquired from undercooked poultry. Treatment consists of treating the underlying cause and symptomatic management with non-steroidal analgesia initially. For symptoms uncontrolled with NSAIDs, intra-articular glucocorticoids are indicated. Following this, systemic steroids can be used; however, they are only required in a minority of patients.

B Azithromycin PO

Azithromycin can be used in the treatment of chlamydia and gonorrhoea but would be unhelpful in the absence of any current infective symptoms, as here.

C IV fLucloxacillin

Flucloxacillin is indicated for an acutely septic joint, although the sterile aspirate indicates this is not the cause in

D Prednisolone PO

Steroids are indicated in the management of knee pain, which does not resolve following treatment with NSAIDs in reactive arthritis. Given the possible adverse effects with systemic administration, intra-articular steroids are used preferentially to PO steroids.

E Methylprednisolone IV

Methylprednisolone is usually used IV for suppression of inflammatory disorders such as relapse of multiple sclerosis or transplant graft rejections. Given possible adverse effects with systemic administration, intra- articular steroids are used preferentially to PO steroids. If systemic steroid administration is required, then PO prednisolone would be preferred over IV methylprednisolone in this case.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman has been admitted from clinic with severe rheumatoid arthritis (RA). She has symptoms of persistent synovitis, despite taking high-dose weekly methotrexate, non-steroidal anti-inflammatories and low-dose prednisolone. The consultant has discussed pros and cons of starting biological therapy. What of the following criteria would rule out infliximab as an option for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Coexistent psoriasis

Psoriasis is a target disease for treatment with anti-TNF agents and data show a consistent improvement in symptoms associated with therapy.

B Coexistent multiple sclerosis

Evidence from intervention trials with anti-TNF agents in inflammatory bowel disease and arthritis have suggested increased risk of new demyelinating diseases in patients prescribed them. The mechanism as to why this happens is unclear, as it is not consistently reflected in animal models of multiple sclerosis. Other contraindications for anti-TNF agents include: Active serious infection ( invasive fungal infection or bacterial infection) Doses >5 mg/kg in patients with moderate-to-severe heart failure (NYHA Class III/IV) Active tuberculosis (patients should also be screened for previous infection before starting therapy). Previous severe hypersensitivity reaction to infliximab or known hypersensitivity to any component of infliximab or to any murine proteins. It would be prudent to note that pregnancy and lactation is not absolute contraindications to infliximab. Infliximab products cross the placenta and can detect up to six months following birth; recommend waiting at least six months following birth before administering of any live vaccine to infants exposed in utero to infliximab

C Asthma

Although TNF is not a target for patients suffering from asthma, anti-TNF agents do not worsen symptoms of asthma.

D Gout

Anti-inflammatory agents may impact on the acute phase of gout, although anti-IL1-based agents probably have the greatest positive effect rather than anti-TNF.

E Glaucoma

Anti-TNF agents have no negative effect on intra-ocular pressure or symptoms of glaucoma.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease comes to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. She complains of increasing bony pains and proximal muscle weakness. Her Crohn’s is currently relatively under control. She is taking azathioprine only and her C-reactive protein (CRP) is only just above the normal range. Her consumption of dietary calcium has been increased since her last operation nine months earlier. She opens her bowels 3–4 times per day. Past surgical history includes three small bowel resections. On examination, her blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg; pulse is 65 bpm and regular. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender, she has the scars from previous surgery, and her body mass index (BMI) is 19 kg/m². She has proximal myopathy affecting the hips and shoulders.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)105 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)8.1 × 10⁹/L4–11 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)167 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)87 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)18 mg/L0–10 mg/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)41 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)195 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Albumin29 g/L35–55 g/L
Calcium2.0 mmol/L2.2–2.6 mmol/L

Which of the following is the most appropriate next intervention?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Calcium supplements

Although calcium supplementation would help correct the low calcium, it is likely the low calcium is a result of vitamin D malabsorption. Therefore, calcium supplements would be not clinically indicated unless adequate vitamin supplementation does not correct the calcium.

B Cholestyramine

Cholestyramine is a treatment option for diarrhoea associated with bile acid malabsorption. It is a binding agent and does not directly affect absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

C Codeine

Codeine is a treatment option for bile acid malabsorption associated diarrhoea and does not directly affect absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

D Increased Azathioprine

The clinical symptoms and blood tests reflect a malabsorption disorder secondary to previous bowel resection, there is no value in increasing the azathioprine dose.

E Vitamin D

This patient is most likely to have malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins due to multiple previous bowel resections. The fat-soluble vitamins are vitamin A, D, E, K. Her symptoms and blood picture are consistent with osteomalacia and vitamin D supplementation will therefore improve her condition.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman complains of severe headache, mainly in the occipital region, as well as irritability, low mood and lack of energy. Her husband informs you that he has noted her to be withdrawn and short-tempered. She also gives a history of a recent increase in hair loss, and joint pains, predominantly in the wrist and knees. She has had amenorrhoea for the last 3 months. She works as a secretary, and is now finding it extremely difficult to cope with both her work and household activities. She and her husband are requesting sick leave. On examination, she looks unwell. Her temperature is 37.5 °C, she is pale and there is an erythematous rash on her face. The joint examination is remarkable for tenderness in the wrists and knees, but no swelling. Cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examination are unrevealing. The neurological examination does not show focal neurological signs or neck stiffness.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)97 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)3.8 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)188 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Neutrophils2.1 × 10⁹/L2.5–7.58 × 10⁹/L
Lymphocytes0.8 × 10⁹/L1.5–3.5 × 10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)88 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour
C-reactive protein (CRP)8.0 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)44 IU/L10–40 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)156 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)50 IU/L5–30 IU/L
ANAPositive
DNA and ENAAwaited
Urine dipstickProtein trace

What is the most likely clinical problem that may explain the above?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Neuropsychiatric lupus

This young lady is in the right demographic to suspect systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), which is suggested by polyarthralgia, hair fall, facial rash and positive ANA. However, the symptoms of headache and mood changes point towards the possibility of neuropsychiatric lupus. Features of neurological disease in lupus range from the common, relatively harmless migraine headache, to major psychotic episodes and grand mal seizures, recognised in some lupus patients. Amenorrhoea is sometimes observed with neuropsychiatric lupus, and may be due to either interference with gonadotrophin release or associated autoimmune ovarian failure.

B Viral meningitis

The history is too protracted, and the non-neurological features (facial rash, hair fall) are more suggestive of connective tissue disease and do not fit with viral meningitis.

C Lupus glomerulonephritis

Lupus glomerulonephritis cannot be completely excluded, but active urinary sediment with proteinuria ++ on dipstick will be more suggestive.

D Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome

Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APLS) can cause headaches and migraines, but also dural sinus thrombosis. APLS should be considered, but is less likely as her platelets are normal and she has psychological features in addition to her severe headache.

E Bacterial meningitis

The history is too protracted, her CRP is normal and there is no meningism.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman presents with episodic discoloration of the fingers of both hands – white followed by a bluish tinge – first noticed 2 years ago. She has otherwise been fit and healthy and denies any previous medical problems. Which of the following investigations would be most useful in determining whether the Raynaud’s is related to vasculitis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Rheumatoid factor (RF) testing

The RF is non-specific and is found in multiple conditions, including infections.

B Antinuclear antibody testing

A close second to nail fold capillaroscopy. Measurement of anti-nuclear antibodies, whilst being non-specific, may provide additional clarification for Raynauds.

C X-ray of the hands

X-rays are likely to be completely normal, even in secondary Rayaud’s associated with connective tissue disease.

D X-ray of the chest

X-ray of the chest is useful to determine whether cervical ribs are present, as a cause of Raynauds, but not to determine any other causes.

E Nail fold capillaroscopy

This young woman has symptoms of Raynaud’s syndrome. It will be important to differentiate between primary and Raynaud’s secondary to connective tissue disease (CTD). The most useful initial assessment must include nail fold capillary loop examination, ideally by capillaroscopy or, if not available, by ophthalmoscope using magnification. Patients with CTD such as systemic sclerosis most often will show a positive ANA and dilated, distorted, missed nail fold capillary loops (i.e. with gaps – areas of drop-out).

questions.question: A 64-year-old man presents to the General Medical Clinic. He is concerned as his wife has pointed out that his ears look different. He has a past medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, recurrent joint pain and steatohepatitis. Aside from the joint pain, he has not noticed anything abnormal in terms of pain or itch. He has otherwise been feeling well, without any other pain or systemic problems. He currently takes ramipril, atorvastatin and amlodipine. A photograph of his right ear is shown below. What is the most appropriate plan for this patient’s management?
options: Staging computed tomography (CT) scan of head and neck
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Excision biopsy of lesion

The lesions presents are not consistent with malignancy. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) can arise on the ears as they are in a sun-exposed area. These lesions are hyperkeratotic lesions which often develop a central ulcer which can bleed and are often itchy. There is also usually only one lesion.

B Staging computed tomography (CT) scan of head and neck

Staging scanning is appropriate when a malignant melanoma has been confirmed. Melanomas are usually characterised by flat, irregular, multichromatic lesions with changing appearance. They are also usually pigmented. If these features were present, the initial step would still be to do a biopsy to confirm the nature of the lesion.

C Prednisolone

Systemic steroid therapy would be an option for acute gout, not for chronic gout.

D Allopurinol

This patient has gouty tophi on his ears. It is likely given this that he has undiagnosed recurrent gout given his history of recurrent joint pain. Gouty tophi are nodular masses of monosodium urate crystals deposited in soft tissue and are a sign of chronic hyperuricaemia. Starting urate-lowering treatment would be appropriate to prevent further attacks of gout. Measuring serum urate would be appropriate to ensure adequate response. As allopurinol is started, he should also be given treatment for acute gout as allopurinol can, in the first instance, precipitate an acute attack.

E Stop ramipril

In most patients with gout, the excess or urate arises from failure of excretion. It is important to stop thiazide diuretics for these patients, but not ramipril. Ramipril is important to maintain renal function by preventing hypertensive nephropathy.

questions.question:
