A 50-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 1-day history of anterolateral chest pain. He noticed the onset of pain while cooking dinner and describes the pain as sharp in nature, made worse on taking in deep breaths. He feels slightly breathless and unable to take full breaths of air. He denies fever or coryza but has a slight residual cough from a viral infection one week ago. His past medical history includes hypertension and hyperlipidaemia, for which he takes amlodipine, ramipril and atorvastatin. He smokes 5–10 cigarettes per day. On examination, his temperature is 36.2 °C. He has a heart rate of 88 bpm, with a blood pressure of 150/89 mmHg. On auscultation, chest sounds are clear, with a respiratory rate of 18 breaths/minute and oxygen saturations of 99% on room air. His heart sounds are normal, with a capillary refill time of < 2 seconds. He has a soft and non-tender abdomen. There is reproducible chest pain on palpation of his sternum and anterior chest wall.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)140 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)9.3 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Neutrophils4.1 × 10⁹/L2.5–7.5 × 10⁹/L
Lymphocytes3.6 × 10⁹/L0.8–5.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)367 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.1 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea5.3 mmol/L1.8–7.1 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)62 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR)69 ml/min/1.73 m60+ ml/min/1.73 m
D-dimer350 ng/L< 400 ng/L
Fibrinogen2.1 g/L2–4 g/L
Troponin14 ng/L0–14 ng/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)9 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Electrocardiogram (ECG) – sinus rhythmChest X-ray – pending

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Costochondritis

This patient has costochondritis characterised by tenderness of the costochondral and chondrosternal joints of the anterior chest wall. Pain may have an acute or gradual onset and can be described as sharp, aching or like a pressure sensation. Exacerbating symptoms include coughing, deep inspiration and physical activity. Before the onset of symptoms, there is often a history of recent illness or strenuous exercise. This patient has reproducible chest pain following a recent viral illness, in addition to normal laboratory investigations, making the diagnosis of costochondritis most likely. A secondary bacterial lower respiratory tract infection may follow from a recent viral illness; pneumonia should be considered in patients presenting with chest pain and shortness of breath after a recent viral infection. This is particularly true following infection with influenza, as pneumonia secondary to Staphylococcus aureus is a well- known complication. However, the presence of normal inflammatory markers and normal chest sounds makes the diagnosis of pneumonia less likely. Pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardial sac often, but not always, triggered by a viral or bacterial illness. Other causes include uraemic pericarditis and post-myocardial infarction pericarditis (Dressler syndrome).

B Pericarditis

The ECG is diagnostic of pericarditis and often shows PR-segment depression and saddle-shaped ST-segment elevation, with reciprocal ST-segment depression in leads aVR and V1. Cardiac enzymes such as troponin may be normal and pericarditis and raised levels indicate damage to the myocardium. The presence of a normal ECG makes the diagnosis of pericarditis less likely.

C Pneumonia

Symptoms include sharp central chest pain that is made worse when lying flat and relieved by sitting forward.

D Pneumothorax

A pneumothorax, particularly secondary pneumothorax, should be considered in a patient with chest pain and shortness of breath and a history of smoking. However, the presence of equal breath sounds bilaterally, makes the diagnosis of a pneumothorax less likely.

E Pulmonary embolism (PE)

PE is an important differential to consider for patients with pleuritic chest pain. However, the absence of tachycardia and hypoxia, along with a negative D-dimer, suggests an alternative diagnosis.

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology Clinic with progressive swelling of both hands and shortness of breath. She has noticed her hands becoming whiter at times for many years. More recently, she has started to experience dyspnoea on exertion of up to 400 yards, with occasional palpitations. The patient has smoked 15 cigarettes a day for 20 years and drinks 14 units of alcohol a week. She currently takes lansoprazole prescribed by her General Practitioner for gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. On examination, her hands reveal evidence of calcinosis. Autoantibodies are checked, which reveal a positive anti-centromere antibody. Which is the most likely cause of this patient’s exertional dyspnoea?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

CREST (specificity > 90%) and pulmonary hypertension. Anti-topoisomerase 1 antibodies are associated with interstitial lung disease and anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies are associated with renal and cardiac involvement, including scleroderma renal crisis. This patient’s signs, symptoms and investigation findings are in keeping with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is not a feature of this condition. Although she has just under a 20 pack-year smoking history, her symptoms are most likely to be related to pulmonary hypertension, which is a common feature of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

B Chronic pulmonary emboli

Although chronic small pulmonary emboli may result in pulmonary hypertension and the respiratory symptoms experienced by this patient, her other symptoms and investigation findings point towards a diagnosis of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

C Congestive cardiac failure

Although cardiac failure may present with dyspnoea on exertion, it is unlikely to present at such a young age without any prior history of cardiac disease. The patient’s other signs and symptoms, along with her positive anti-centromere antibodies, point towards a diagnosis of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis, of which pulmonary hypertension is a feature.

D Interstitial lung disease

Fibrosing interstitial lung disease is the main differential here. However, this is more commonly seen in systemic sclerosis where there are positive anti-topoisomerase 1 autoantibodies. Interstitial lung disease may cause a cough, exertional dyspnoea and fatigue but is unlikely to be associated with palpitations.

E Pulmonary artery hypertension

This patient has findings in keeping with a diagnosis of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Scleroderma is a rare multisystem chronic condition of unknown cause. It is characterised by tissue fibrosis, small blood vessel vasculopathy (Raynaud’s phenomenon) and autoimmunity. Diffuse scleroderma is characterised by both cutaneous and visceral involvement, with rapid skin thickening on the extremities, face and trunk. Limited scleroderma has a lower risk of early visceral involvement; pulmonary artery hypertension is a significant risk but usually appears later in the disease process, such as in this patient. The features of calcinosis, Raynaud’s phenomenon, oesophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly and telangiectasia meant that it was historically referred to as CREST. Limited scleroderma or limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis is the preferred term when the patient does not have all of the features of CREST. Anti-centromere antibodies are most strongly associated with

questions.question: A 71-year-old man is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic with pain over his left hip and pelvis. Previously very active, he is now limited to walking only a few hundred yards due to pain. Past medical history of note includes hypertension, which is treated with felodipine. On examination, his BP is 135/70 mmHg, with pulse 70/min and regular. He has pain over the left hip, and flexion and external rotation are limited by pain. His GP has arranged an X-ray of the hip, which reveals evidence of osteolysis and new bone formation around both the femoral head and the pelvis. Which of the following is most likely to be abnormal?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Calcium

Calcium in patients with Paget’s remains in the normal range for the majority of patients, unless there is a prolonged period of bed rest, where minor elevations may be seen.

B Alkaline phosphatase

The X-ray appearance is typical of Paget’s disease. In patients with Paget’s, other markers of bone turnover, apart from alkaline phosphatase, are usually in the normal range. Alkaline phosphatase is a useful marker of disease activity and of response to bisphosphonates, with a fall in alkaline phosphatase correlating with a reduction in disease activity. Over the longer term, bisphosphonates may not be completely effective; one study suggested that despite the use of etidronate, disease progression occurred in 28% of individuals.

C Vitamin D

Vitamin D elevation is seen in patients with sarcoidosis and symptomatic hypercalcaemia, and in those who take excess exogenous vitamin D.

D Phosphate

Elevations in phosphate are seen in hypoparathyroidism and in those with renal impairment, rather than those with Paget’s.

E Parathyroid hormone (PTH)

Hyperparathyroidism is not usually associated with single joint destruction, and is normal in patients with Paget’s disease.

questions.question: A 38-year-old male postgraduate student from Hong Kong presents to his general practitioner (GP) complaining of sudden-onset left ear pain, and with an inability to sleep on the affected side. He reports that he is feeling very low because he has had a number of health problems since coming to this country 6 months ago. On further questioning, he admits to having general aches and pains, including pains in various joints over this time. He reports that both his eyes are red all the time but that anti-allergy drops bought from the chemist have had no effect. He has also had a couple of nose bleeds, which is a first for him and which he blames on the increased pollution in the air, which he also feels is responsible for the hoarseness in his voice. He denies any known medical problems and, apart from analgesics, he is not on any regular medication. Positive findings on clinical examination include left auricular chondritis, bilateral eyelid oedema and bilateral mild episcleritis, tenderness to palpation over the anterior trachea and pain on palpation over the costochondral joints. The GP orders some blood tests and X-rays, including rheumatoid factor, which is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Relapsing polychondritis

This young man has inflammation of cartilaginous structures – the pinna (red, painful ear), nasal septum (epistaxis) and larynx (hoarse voice), as well as chostochondritis and the C-rings of the trachea, consistent with relapsing polychondritis (RP). There is no gender difference in the distribution of the disease, and although it can occur at any age it is most common in the fifth decade. The patient’s reported symptoms depend on the area of the body affected. General symptoms include intermittent fever and weight loss, but other more specific symptoms include sudden onset of ear pain with an inability to sleep on the affected side, diminished hearing, mono- or polyarthritis, back pain, myalgias, mild epistaxis, saddle-shaped nose, redness of the eyes indicative of conjunctivitis, episcleritis and/or scleritis, hoarseness of the voice and recurrent respiratory infections. There are no specific diagnostic laboratory findings in patients with RP, but the non-specific indicators of inflammation (ESR, CRP) are often elevated. No specific therapy exists for RP, but the goal of treatment is to control the patient’s symptoms and to preserve the integrity of the affected cartilaginous structures. The mainstay of treatment is systemic corticosteroids. It is important in these patients to investigate for the presence of other concurrent autoimmune diseases.

B Reactive arthritis

Cogan syndrome is a rare chronic inflammatory autoimmune-mediated disorder characterised by inflammation of the ears and eyes. The pathophysiology is poorly understood, but the immunological theory is based on the release of auto-antibodies against corneal, inner ear and endothelial antigens, and of anti-nuclear cytoplasmic auto-antibodies (ANCA). Preceding infection may also be implicated but again the exact mechanism is unclear.

C Granulomatosis with polyangitis (GPA)

This condition should, however, be considered in the differential. Ear pain and chostochondritis do not occur with GPA. GPA is a rare multi-system autoimmune condition with a wide spectrum of symptoms including lethargy, ongoing rhinitis and sinusitis, arthritis, lung, eye and ENT manifestations. Hallmark histological features are a necrotising granulomatous inflammation and pauci-immune vasculitis in small and medium-sized vessels. Ear pain, epistaxis and hoarse voice are not features of reactive arthritis. Reactive arthritis is a systemic inflammatory disorder characterised by an aseptic oligoarthritis, triggered by infections arising most commonly from the genitourinary and gastrointestinal systems. A history of urethritis/dysuria and conjunctivitis completes the reactive arthritis triad.

D Cogan’s syndrome

Cogan syndrome can lead to vision difficulty, hearing loss and dizziness. The inner ear is affected, leading to hearing loss in Cogan syndrome, whereas in this case the cartilaginous pinna is affected resulting in a red, swollen, painful ear.

E Polyarteritis nodosa

This is a rare medium-sized vessel vasculitis, usually leading to mesenteric ischaemia and mononeuritis multiplex. Its presentation is usually of acute onset, with non-specific symptoms including fatigue, myalgia, arthralgia and fever. Multi-system involvement may occur with wide and varied symptoms. However, the symptoms described in this patient are more consistent with relapsing polychondritis.

questions.question:
A 17-year-old girl presents with a 10-day history of feeling unwell. She describes fever, a rash on her body that has now cleared, and currently has pain in her left knee. She tells you that she has had a few eye infections in the past that cleared up and often gets swollen joints, as she is a keen gymnast. She takes no regular medications and has no allergies. She has not been abroad recently. She has previously had similar episodes in the past affecting both her knees and has felt that other joints were involved too. These have been episodic in nature over the last 2 years. She had seen her GP at the time who wanted to investigate with blood tests, but she declined due to needle-phobia and managed her pain with over the counter ibuprofen. On examination she is thin. Her temperature is 38.7 °C. She has cervical lymphadenopathy. Her blood pressure is 110/80 mm/Hg; pulse 106 bpm regular. Heart sounds are normal with no murmurs. Auscultation of the chest is unremarkable. There is a splenic tip palpable on abdominal examination. Her left knee is swollen and tender and there is evidence of a small effusion.

Investigations are as follows:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)118 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)13 × 10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)190 × 10⁹/L150 - 400 × 10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)90 mm/h1 - 20 mm/h
Blood filmNAD
Joint aspirate Microscopy, Culture & Sensitivity No growth after 48 h
Urine microscopy and cultureNo abnormality detected
Paul–Bunnell test Negative
Three days later, while in hospital, she develops painful wrists and pain on neck movement. Cardiovascular examination reveals a new friction rub but no evidence of cardiac failure.

Which diagnosis should be considered?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Lyme's Disease

The absence of a tick bite and erythema migrans makes this diagnosis unlikely, and it would also not explain the joint effusion.

B Rubella

This is a very unlikely diagnosis in general due to vaccination, and also does not explain the presence of pericarditis or joint effusion.

C Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

The initial presentation with fever, pain and swelling of the left knee with a prodromal history makes a diagnosis of infective arthritis important to exclude. Occasionally acute leukaemia can cause a pyogenic arthritis but the normal blood film excludes this. The progression of symptoms suggests a systemic disease. The most important differentials to consider are therefore rheumatic fever, juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) and rheumatoid arthritis. The history of similar joint problems with a chronic relapsing course starting before the age of 16 makes missed JIA a strong possibility. Cervical spine involvement is more common in JIA. SLE is a multisystem autoimmune disease working in multiple immunological ways including immune complex formation and deposition and complement activation. It is relapsing-remitting with variable symptoms including fatigue, malaise, fever with lymphadenopathy, weight loss Raynaud’s and migraine. It is often associated with a malar rash and a discoid rash, as well as non-erosive arthritis of peripheral joints. However, the presentation is very early for this diagnosis and the joint involvement is far more likely to be of small joints and symmetrical.

D Systemic lupus erythematosus

Lyme disease is a tick-borne infection of Borrelia burgdorferi causing erythema migrans at the site of infection, which expands. It causes systemic features as well, including fatigue, myalgia, myocarditis, arthralgia and fever.

E Infectious mononucleosis

Mononucleosis is caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and following 4-5 weeks incubation causes symptoms in adolescents. It is commonly contracted in early childhood and causes no symptoms there. It can a cause fever, sore throat and lymphadenopathy, as well as splenomegaly. A negative Paul–Bunnell test makes infectious mononucleosis unlikely. It would also not explain cardiac or arthritic involvement.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man presents to the general practitioner after returning from a 1-week holiday in Thailand. He complains of pain on passing urine, and cloudy urine that looks like pus on occasions. There is also joint pain predominantly affecting the knees and ankles, and itchy eyes. On examination, there appears to be a psoriatic-type rash affecting the feet. Given the likely diagnosis, which one of the following treatments would best fit with the management of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Methotrexate 2.5 mg po weekly

This patient has reactive arthritis, which is addressed by treating the underlying infection and NSAIDs for

B Azathioprine

Explanation as for Methotrexate 2.5 mg po weekly.

C Doxycycline 100 mg bd

This patient has reactive arthritis, which is a form of seronegative arthritis caused by a remote gastrointestinal or urogenital infection. Pathogens include Chlamydia trachomatis, Yersinia, Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, E. coli, Clostridium difficile and Chlamydia pneumoniae. The social history and suggestion of keratoderma blennorrhagica would implicate Chlamydia infection.

D Prednisolone 40 mg po daily

Oral glucocorticoids are not suggested in the treatment of reactive arthritis, but intra-articular steroid injections can be used in those who do not respond to oral NSAIDs.

E Coal tar skin creams

The psoriatic-type rash in this patient is more likely keratoderma blennorrhagica, given the history. This can be treated with topical steroids or salicylates.

questions.question:
A 73-year-old woman with a history of previous Colles’ fracture presents to the Emergency Department with severe lower back pain. She says she slipped getting out of the bath and the pain began to get much more severe the following morning and has not been relieved by regular paracetamol. She takes medication for hypertension and asthma but is otherwise well. On examination, her BP is 122/82 mmHg and her heart rate 70 bpm and regular. Heart sounds are normal and her chest is clear. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender and her BMI is 22 kg/m². She is very tender over the L4 vertebra.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)125 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)7.9 × 10⁹/L4–11 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)191 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine105 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Calcium (Ca²⁺)2.21 mmol/L2.20–2.60 mmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)105 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Glucose5.2 mmol/L3.5–5.5 mmol/L
Lumbar spine X-ray: Compression fracture of L4.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step with respect to prophylaxis against further fractures?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Calcitonin

Calcitonin is indicated for short-term therapy only in situations where acute bone loss might occur, such as in patients immobilised with a fracture, and for hypercalcaemia of malignancy. Long-term use is avoided because of increased risk for osteosarcoma.

B Calcium and vitamin D

This would be considered an inappropriate option for the treatment of osteoporosis used in isolation because other options, proven to be more effective with respect to fracture prevention, are available.

C Denosumab

Denosumab is a RANK ligand inhibitor which downregulates osteoclast activity. It is indicated for patients with severe osteoporosis (a T score below –4.5) and where other therapies are unsuitable or not tolerated.

D Ibandronate

This patient requires treatment to prevent further osteoporotic fracture. Bisphosphonates are proven to reduce both incident vertebral and hip fractures in a number of outcome studies. In younger patients, alternative options and drug holidays may be considered because of the risk of adynamic bone disease with long-term use. They are also not a first-choice option in patients with significant gastro-oesophageal reflux disease due to local inflammation associated with their use.

E Teriparatide

Teriparatide is a recombinant parathyroid hormone analogue. Like denosumab, it is indicated for the treatment of severe osteoporosis. It is less convenient than a number of other options as it is delivered by daily subcutaneous injection.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man presents with an acutely red, tender, left knee joint. He has a long history of hypertension, which has been well controlled over a number of years with bendroflumethiazide and amlodipine. There is no history of recent injury. The pain has been severe for 2 days, and on examination, the joint is red, warm and tender. There is swelling and a small effusion. The knee joint is aspirated, and the aspirate sent to the lab for analysis. Below is an image of the aspirate when examined under a microscope using polarised light.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)140 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)14.0 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)180 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)145 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.2 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea6.0 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)100 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)10 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)70 mm/hour< 10 mm/hour
Knee joint aspirateWhite blood cells 2000/µl

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Meniscus tear

A meniscal tear would cause a swollen, painful knee joint, but the patient would provide a history of recent injury to the knee, with progressive increase in swelling over a few days. With more severe injury, the patient may experience locking of the knee. This patient has no history of knee injury, and a warm, red joint is not consistent with a meniscal tear.

B Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)

Gout and pseudogout cannot be reliably distinguished on purely clinical grounds. The synovial fluid would be expected to show the presence of crystals. In gout, needle-shaped intracellular and extracellular crystals of monosodium urate appear. When examined with a polarising filter, these are yellow when aligned parallel to the axis of the red compensator, but they turn blue when aligned across the direction of polarisation (ie they exhibit negative birefringence), as seen in the image. In pseudogout, calcium pyrophosphate (CPP) crystals appear, these being shorter and often rhomboidal. Under a polarising filter, CPP crystals do not change colour, according to their alignment relative to the direction of the red compensator. In pseudogout, radiography may show chondrocalcinosis, which is useful in differentiating between the two conditions. However, of the five options provided, gout is the most likely diagnosis in this scenario. RA is very unlikely to present as monoarthritis of the knee and is usually a small joint polyarthritis affecting the hands.

C Gout

This patient has risk factors for gout (middle-aged man, on a diuretic), and therefore, gout is the most likely explanation in this scenario. The low potassium level is consistent with the use of bendroflumethiazide, a drug that predisposes the patient to gout (but not pseudogout), and the inflammatory markers support this. Bendroflumethiazide is not the first-line treatment for hypertension, but the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines recommend that patients who are already taking bendroflumethiazide with well- controlled hypertension continue this treatment.

D Septic arthritis

Whenever a patient has monoarthritis, the clinician should always consider joint sepsis, as it is very important not to miss this diagnosis. However, in this case, the relatively low number of pus cells is against a diagnosis of septic arthritis; most septic joints have a WCC of > 50 000/µl, with > 75% of polymorphonuclear leukocytes.

E Osteoarthritis (OA)

OA is not correct, because of the acute history and very high levels of inflammatory markers. OA is insidious in onset and is associated with normal levels of inflammatory markers.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man presents with a rash on his back, face and scalp, which has appeared over the past year or so. The rash began as dry, red patches, which increased in size and became scaly. He is particularly concerned, as the rash has been associated with some hair loss on his scalp, which has not regrown. The rash has been worse over the summer months, which he has spent with family abroad. On examination, you see the rash pictured below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE)

This is a typical presentation of DLE, the most common type of cutaneous lupus, characterised by plaques on the face, scalp and occasionally generalised rash on the chest or back. The rash is photosensitive and classically associated with scarring alopecia, which is a major differentiating feature in this condition.

B Pityriasis versicolor (PV)

PV is a common yeast infection causing hypopigmented irregular patches, frequently on the chest or back. The rash in this image is hyperpigmented and associated with scarring alopecia. PV is not particularly photosensitive, though loss of pigment can become more marked when adjacent skin becomes tanned.

C Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT)

PCT is the most common type of porphyria and is caused by a defective enzyme (uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase), leading to a disorder in haematological production. This manifests as fragility of the skin, particularly on the back of the hands, and photosensitivity. While the rash in this question is photosensitive, PCT is more commonly associated with sores or blisters, with the formation of milia as the blisters heal. PCT does not cause scarring alopecia.

D Psoriasis

This rash does appear to form scaly plaques akin to psoriasis; however, the history of photosensitivity and scarring alopecia is incompatible with the diagnosis of psoriasis.

E Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

SLE is a multi-system disorder featuring a wide range of symptoms, including photosensitive rash. However, to seal a diagnosis, one would expect more systemic symptoms, including arthralgia, mouth ulcers, or renal impairment. Moreover, DLE is significantly more common than SLE.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man who lives alone presents with right-sided shoulder pain after falling out of bed. He had a previous history of asthma, angina and poorly controlled diabetes. Upon presentation, his shoulder X-ray showed mild degenerative changes only. He was started on basic analgesia and physiotherapy. After three years, he has lost function to his right shoulder, with mild pain. He has significant limitation to all movements in the shoulder on examination. There is unilateral swelling and erythema of the joint. He is otherwise well and apyrexial. Investigations: White cell count (WCC) 5.2 × 10⁹/L (4–11 × 10⁹/L) Joint aspiration No organisms seen An X-ray of the shoulder is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Adhesive capsulitis

Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) is a common cause of shoulder pain and may happen spontaneously or following a rotator cuff injury. However, X-rays are commonly normal in this condition. Therefore, the X-ray in this case effectively rules out adhesive capsulitis.

B Charcot joint

Neuropathic (Charcot) arthropathy is most frequently associated with the foot or ankle. However, it may occur in any joint, and in the upper limb, it may be associated with syringomyelia. This X-ray shows resorption of the proximal aspect of the humerus, seen in severe Charcot joint.

C Osteomyelitis

Osteomyelitis is an important differential in this case. However, the X-ray features of osteomyelitis include regional osteopenia and a periosteal reaction, unlike the almost complete resorption of the humerus seen in the case. Trauma is a risk factor for osteomyelitis; however, patients are classically febrile and in significant pain, pointing away from osteomyelitis.

D Septic arthritis

Septic arthritis is another essential diagnosis to consider in a patient with a red and swollen joint. However, in this stem, there are no organisms seen in the joint aspiration; the patient is well and afebrile, and the pain is mild.

E Shoulder dislocation

The X-ray in this case features almost complete resorption of the humeral head, very different to the features of shoulder dislocation.

questions.question: A 70-year-old woman with brittle asthma presents with left hip and groin pain. It is very painful to bear weight. An X-ray of her hip reveals no evidence of a fracture. She is confused and cannot give a history. On examination, she is afebrile and there is no redness or warmth around the hip. You notice that her fingers appear deformed. What investigation will give the definitive diagnosis for her hip pain?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Inflammatory markers

Although this lady is likely to have rheumatoid arthritis, as suggested by the swan-neck deformity of the fourth and fifth fingers, inflammatory markers are unlikely to help – the history suggests a monoarthritis but dissuades you from a septic arthritis, with the absence of fever or erythema.

B MRI hip

The most likely diagnosis is of avascular necrosis of the hip, given the clues to oral steroid use – ‘brittle’ asthma as well as rheumatoid arthritis. An MRI is the diagnostic imaging technique of choice.

C Auto-antibodies

Auto-antibodies may help you confirm a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis, but would not help delineate the cause of her acute hip pain.

D Arthroscopy

Arthroscopy is very invasive and unnecessary in this case, to diagnose avascular necrosis.

E X-ray knee

It is always important to think of the joint below (and above if applicable), as pain may be referred. However, in this case with groin pain and likely long-term steroid use, the most likely diagnosis is avascular necrosis of the hip. The hip is a common site, as it is supplied by an end-artery.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 1-month history of joint pains and sore, red eyes. She has no significant past medical history and is taking no medication. She smokes 10–15 cigarettes per day and drinks one bottle of wine over the weekend. Examination reveals normal cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal systems. Joint examination reveals tenderness in her knees, but mainly in her ankle joints, with a reduced range of movement and swelling.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea5.0 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)60 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Bilirubin12 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)100 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT)35 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Corrected Calcium (Ca²⁺)2.70 mmol/L2.20–2.60 mmol/L
White Cell Count (WCC)10 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Haemoglobin (Hb)130 g/L115–155 g/L
Platelets (PLT)170 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Chest X-ray:

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Granulomatosis with polyangiitis

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis typically presents with upper and/or lower respiratory tract symptoms, including haemoptysis, epistaxis and shortness of breath. Extrapulmonary symptoms can be present; however, these tend to include vasculitis and cranial nerve lesions, rather than arthritis.

B Primary hyperparathyroidism

This patient’s clinical features (arthritis, hilar lymphadenopathy) are not explained by primary hyperparathyroidism. The only feature that fits is hypercalcaemia.

C Sarcoidosis

Sarcoidosis is the most likely diagnosis because this patient has ankle synovitis (which is quite classical for sarcoidosis), hypercalcaemia on blood testing and hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray. Note that Löfgren syndrome is an acute form of sarcoidosis, with erythema nodosum, hilar lymphadenopathy and polyarthralgia or polyarthritis. Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) levels may be elevated; however, this is non- specific for sarcoidosis. Across the range of patients with sarcoidosis, hypercalcaemia is seen in up to 20%.

D Small cell lung carcinoma

Although this patient smokes, the lack of symptoms of cough, haemoptysis, shortness of breath and weight loss makes lung malignancy less likely.

E Tuberculosis

Tuberculosis typically presents with chest X-ray signs of a Ghon focus (a lung lesion typically located in the apical lobe, composed of macrophages). It does not typically present with hilar lymphadenopathy, as seen on this patient's X-ray.

questions.question: A 67-year-old woman with long-standing erosive rheumatoid arthritis is referred by her general practitioner (GP) for further management. She has bilateral lower limb swelling and difficult to manage hypertension. Current medication includes low dose corticosteroids, methotrexate, ramipril, aspirin and atorvastatin. On examination, her blood pressure is 149/82 mmHg, pulse is 78 bpm regular. She has bilateral pitting oedema but her chest is clear. There is hepatomegaly on abdominal examination. Investigations: Hb 110 g/L WCC 7.8 × 10⁹/L PLT 190 × 10⁹/L Na 139 mmol/L K 4.9 mmol/L Creatinine 199 μmol/L Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 44 mm/hr Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 54 U/l Alkaline phosphatase 189 U/l 24-h urinary protein 3.1g Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Systemic inflammatory amyloidosis

The hepatomegaly, heavy proteinuria with raised alkaline phosphatase is a strong indicator towards amyloid infiltration. Secondary inflammatory amyloidosis occurs due to increased circulating levels of serum amyloid A, which is an acute phase reactant. The raised ESR seen here is an indication of ongoing inflammation related to her rheumatoid disease. While colchicine is of value in reducing amyloid deposition in familial Mediterranean fever, there is no evidence it has a positive effect in amyloidosis related to underlying systemic inflammation. Treatment should focus on intensive control of the underlying cause; her rheumatoid disease.

B Methotrexate toxicity

Methotrexate toxicity can cause myelosuppression (but her FBC is fine) and hepatotoxicity (her ALT is only mildly elevated). It is not associated with hepatomegaly or nephrotic syndrome. Rheumatoid arthritis drugs that may cause nephrotic syndrome include penicillamine and gold.

C Rheumatoid vasculitis

Rheumatoid vasculitis very rarely affects the kidneys, but usually causes cutaneous (purpuric rashes) and neurological (mononeuritis multiplex) manifestations.

D Minimal change disease

Although minimal change disease might explain her nephrotic syndrome, it would not explain hepatomegaly.

E Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

This lady has known rheumatoid arthritis and therefore is unlikely to then develop an entirely different disease later. The key to knowing that she did not have an arthritis as part of SLE that evolved later on, is the finding that she had erosions, which are strongly suggestive that the original diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis was

questions.question: A 64-year-old patient with a long history of rheumatoid arthritis attends the clinic for review. She is managed on low-dose methotrexate, folic acid and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents for her disease, but has noticed a worsening in her rheumatoid nodules over the past few months and has developed dry eyes most recently. On examination, she has splenomegaly. Investigations reveal a low total white count of 3.4 × 10⁹/L; she is also anaemic, with haemoglobin of 98 g/L and a platelet count of 105 × 10⁹/L. Which of the following interventions would be most appropriate initially in this case?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Stop methotrexate therapy

This is not methotrexate toxicity but Felty syndrome. The key is the worsening of RA features and splenomegaly.

B Folinic acid rescue

This is not methotrexate toxicity but Felty syndrome. Folinic acid rescue is the treatment for methotrexate toxicity.

C Splenectomy

Splenectomy is one option in patients with Felty syndrome who fail to respond to medical intervention.

D Busulphan

This patient does not have development of lymphoma, but rather Felty syndrome.

E Pulsed corticosteroid therapy

This patient has Felty syndrome, as evidenced by splenomegaly and worsening of extra-articular manifestations in a patient with a long-standing history of rheumatoid arthritis. This, coupled with the low white count, is highly suggestive of Felty syndrome, which has a 60–70% female predominance and is usually recognised from the fifth decade onwards in patients who have had rheumatoid arthritis for an average of 10 years or more. Pulsed corticosteroid and/or cyclophosphamide therapy may be effective in raising neutrophil counts, as may appropriate switching/intensification of DMARD therapy for the rheumatoid.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old woman presents with intensely painful fingers on going outdoors during the autumn and winter months. She reports the same problem if she washes her hands in cold water. Her fingers go pale and blue- tinged, and later become erythematous and are burning and prickly. Examination in the clinic is unremarkable.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)137 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)4.8 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)188 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Neutrophils2.1 × 10⁹/L2.5–7.58 × 10⁹/L
Lymphocytes1.8 × 10⁹/L1.5–3.5 × 10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)18 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour
C-reactive protein (CRP)21 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)28 IU/L10–40 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)101 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)15 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Glucose5.5 mmol/L3.5–5.5 mmol/L
Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH)2.0 µU/L0.17–3.2 µU/L
Creatine kinase (CK)70 IU/L23–175 IU/L
Anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA)Negative

What is the best initial medical treatment for this lady?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Nifedipine MR

Extensive screening has failed to establish an underlying cause for this lady’s Raynaud’s, so she has primary Raynaud’s phenomenon or Raynaud’s disease. Primary Raynaud’s is not usually associated with increased mortality or morbidity, although occasionally necrosis of the affected extremity may occur. Clearly, in patients presenting with this symptom picture, it is crucial to carry out an extensive screen for underlying autoimmune or metabolic disease as in this case, as therapy should be tailored to any underlying condition. Primary Raynaud’s commonly presents in the second or third decade of life, and prevalence is slightly higher in women than men – put at around 5% depending on case series. Treatment of choice is with vasodilating calcium-channel antagonists such as nifedipine modified/sustained release (MR/SR) or angiotensin II receptor blockers such as losartan.

B Atenolol

Beta blockers such as atenolol may precipitate a worsening of Raynaud’s symptoms, as they may cause vasoconstriction.

C Ramipril

There is no evidence that ACE inhibitors improve symptoms of Raynaud’s, and there is no indication in primary Raynaud’s. There is some evidence to support the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) or angiotensin II–receptor blockers (ARBs), such as losartan. However, it is unclear why the mechanisms of why ARBs are advantageous over ACE inhibitors.

D Prednisolone

Steroids do not improve symptoms of Raynaud’s, and there is no indication in primary Raynaud’s. Steroids may occasionally be used in secondary Raynaud’s where there is an underlying inflammatory process driving the condition, e.g. in SLE.

E Aspirin

There is no evidence that aspirin improves the symptoms of Raynaud’s. Multiple antithrombotic agents, including aspirin, dipyridamole, anticoagulants and thrombolytic therapy, have been used in patients with Raynaud’s phenomenon in whom ulceration and thrombosis have occurred. The benefit of antiplatelet therapy is not well studied, but such therapy is often used in cases of secondary Raynaud’s phenomenon when there is a risk of thrombosis. Long-term anticoagulation in the absence of a hypercoagulable state is not recommended.

questions.question: A 56-year-old man presents to his doctor for review. He has been suffering particularly from increased bony pain around his lower back and pelvic region over the past few months. Some degree of hearing loss was diagnosed two years ago. Blood testing reveals normal calcium levels but alkaline phosphatase is raised. X-rays reveal skull features consistent with Paget’s disease, and increased activity on bone scanning is seen in the lumbar vertebrae and pelvis. You commence bisphosphonate treatment. Which of the following represents the most appropriate way to monitor disease activity in this man?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A 3-monthly alkaline phosphatase levels

Alkaline phosphatase levels can take 3-4 months to normalise following treatment.

B 6-monthly alkaline phosphatase levels

The goals of therapy in Paget’s disease are to normalise bone turnover and achieve an alkaline phosphatase as a marker of this, in the normal range if possible. Bisphosphonates have become the mainstay of therapy, with daily, weekly, monthly and intravenous intermittent formulations now all possibilities for treatment. It appears that the more aggressive initial therapy is, then the longer a period of remission may be achieved. Alkaline phosphatase, as a non-invasive method, appears to be the best way to monitor disease activity. Levels should be checked at 6 months, and subsequently every 6-12 months.

C 6-monthly acid phosphatase levels

Serum total acid phosphatase is an osteoclastic enzyme that may be elevated in active Paget’s disease, but is not as reliable in males as it can also be raised in prostate cancer.

D 6-monthly calcium levels

Calcium is normal in Paget’s disease.

E Yearly isotope bone scan

It is unclear whether normalisation of appearances on isotope bone scan correlates to clinical outcome. It is therefore difficult to justify the use of serial bone scans to monitor treatment in view of the radiation dose

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman complains of severe pain and aching in her fingers and toes on going out into cold weather. She reports a triad of initial whitening of the fingers resulting from vasospasm, followed by blue discoloration and then reddening and pain. She is currently taking atenolol 50 mg po daily for hypertension and takes methysergide for intermittent migraine. She has a history of reflux nephropathy and her creatinine is 180 μg/L. Her methysergide is discontinued. Which other intervention would be most appropriate for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Start isosorbide dinitrate

NSAIDs are contraindicated given her kidney disease and would not improve her Raynaud’s symptoms in any

B Stop atenolol and start ramipril

Both methysergide and atenolol are possible causes of Raynaud’s phenomenon, or can exacerbate existing Raynaud’s as described here. Other causes include ergotamine, vinblastine, bleomycin and oral contraceptives.

C Start prednisolone 40 mg po daily

There is no evidence for nitrates in improving Raynaud’s symptoms. There are no features of underlying connective tissue disease and this may well be primary Raynaud’s or related to medications. Raynaud’s phenomenon has many causes, including systemic sclerosis, mixed connective tissue disease, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), rheumatoid arthritis, polycythemia and thromboangiitis obliterans.

D Start diclofenac 50 mg po tds

ACE inhibitors also have the best evidence for reno-protection where there is underlying autoimmune pathology. Calcium channel antagonists such as nifedipine may be of value in improving symptoms.

E Start verapamil

Although verapamil is a calcium channel blocker it is not used for Raynaud’s, unlike nifedipine (and even

questions.question: A 66-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner with a 2-week history of progressive shoulder pain. She finds it particularly difficult to get dressed in the morning when her pain is at its worst. She feels generally weak and fatigued and has lost approximately 2 kg in weight. She has no past medical history of note. On examination, she has a temperature of 37.8 °C. Her heart rate is 90 bpm and regular, with a blood pressure of 127/77 mmHg. On auscultation, her heart sounds are normal, with vesicular breath sounds bilaterally. She has a soft and non-tender abdomen, with no palpable organomegaly. There is bilateral proximal muscle stiffness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Adhesive capsulitis

Adhesive capsulitis, or ‘frozen shoulder’, is the gradual onset of pain and stiffness of the shoulder joint. It is more common in middle-aged women. However, usually, only one shoulder is affected. Bilateral shoulder pain and stiffness should raise suspicion of an alternative diagnosis. Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain syndrome that more commonly affects women. It is characterised by widespread pain that can frequently fail to improve with regular analgesia. Other illnesses often coexist with fibromyalgia such as irritable bowel syndrome, tension headache and atypical chest pain. Unlike PMR, fibromyalgia is not an inflammatory disease and the intensity of the symptoms in the morning that improve throughout the day suggests an alternative diagnosis.

B Fibromyalgia

Hyperthyroidism and other endocrine diseases such as Cushing’s disease can cause proximal myopathy. This patient presents with additional symptoms which could indicate hyperthyroidism, including weight loss.

C Hyperthyroidism

However, proximal muscle pain and stiffness indicate an inflammatory cause of this patient’s symptoms, in contrast to myopathy that typically causes muscle weakness, but less likely pain or stiffness.

D Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR)

Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is an inflammatory condition that more commonly presents in women over the age of 60 years. It has similarities with the large vessel vasculitis temporal or giant cell arteritis (GCA), and if visual symptoms are present, GCA should be considered, along with urgent referral to Ophthalmology. PMR tends to have a rapid onset and is characterised by proximal muscle pain and stiffness which is worse in the morning and improves throughout the day. It should not be confused with polymyositis or diseases that cause proximal myopathy which causes proximal muscle weakness. The treatment of choice is long-term steroidal

E Polymyositis

Polymyositis is an inflammatory muscle disease associated with inflammation and weakness of proximal muscles. Proximal muscle ache may also be a symptom. However, morning stiffness is not a feature of polymyositis and is more suggestive of PMR.

questions.question: You are seeing a 21-year-old man with a 3-year history of inflammatory back pain. You make a presumptive diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis (AS). You order X-rays of the lumbosacral spine, sacroiliac joints and HLA B27. Which of the following statements is correct with regard to HLA B27?
options: It can be used as screening test for AS in the general population
The likelihood of a positive test depends on the racial and ethnic background of the patient
The test helps distinguish AS from other spondyloarthropathies
HLA B27 is essential for the diagnosis of AS
Acute anterior uveitis is relatively more common in B27-negative than –positive patients
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A It can be used as screening test for AS in the general population

Although HLA B27 may be helpful in diagnosis, 10% of the asymptomatic healthy normal population may be HLA B27 positive and therefore it cannot be used as a screening test.

B The likelihood of a positive test depends on the racial and ethnic background of the patient

The sensitivity and specificity of the test depend on the racial and ethnic background of the patient. The prevalence of HLA B27 varies among ethnic groups and races. Inuits have been shown to have the highest frequency of the gene (25–40%), with an overall prevalence of spondyloarthropathies between 2 and 4%. HLA B27 frequency is only 8–9% in people from Holland and Germany. Accordingly, the prevalence of spondyloarthropathies (2%) is lower than in Inuit.

C The test helps distinguish AS from other spondyloarthropathies

HLA B27 positivity does not distinguish between the axial spondyloarthropathies.

D HLA B27 is essential for the diagnosis of AS

Most AS patients do not need HLA B 27 testing if they have certain clinical and radiological features. Patients can fulfil the criteria for AS without testing positive for HLA B27.

E Acute anterior uveitis is relatively more common in B27-negative than –positive patients

Acute anterior uveitis is more common in B27-positive than -negative patients.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old Japanese city banker presents with recurrent mouth ulcers. He was seen by the oral surgeons, who prescribed chlorhexidine mouthwashes and oral aciclovir. He has used prednisolone lozenges in the past with good effect. More recently, the ulcers have been occurring more frequently. In the last two days, he has felt pain at the tip of his penis, particularly when having sexual intercourse. He has also felt increasingly tired recently, to the point that he has given up playing football. He denies any weight loss and his appetite is unchanged. He has a history of irritable bowel disease. He also remembers treating an eye condition with steroid drops a year or two previously. He is currently taking oxytetracycline prescribed by his general practitioner (GP) for acne. On examination, there are multiple aphthous ulcers in the oral cavity. There is also a small aphthous ulcer on the tip of the penis. Cardiovascular, respiratory and neurological examinations are unremarkable. Abdominal examination reveals mild, diffuse tenderness but no masses. Rectal examination reveals no abnormality.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)120 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)9.0 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)400 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.0 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea6.8 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)100 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)20 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour
Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA)Negative
Anti-dsDNA antibody (AdsDNAA) Negative

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Crohn’s disease

Oral ulceration is a common feature of SLE, but genital ulcers are not. Lupus antibodies are negative and Behçet’s disease is a much more likely explanation for the multiple features described.

B Behçet’s syndrome

This is a chronic multi-system disease, most prevalent in the Mediterranean, Middle East and Japan. It has been associated with various HLA types including B12, -B51 and -B5. There is no specific diagnostic test, making it a diagnosis of exclusion. Its features can overlap with those of Crohn’s disease, and therefore the latter must be excluded. It is a systemic vasculitic disorder involving arteries and veins, with a tendency to thrombosis. In over 90% of cases there are painful oral aphthous ulcers, in over 70% genital aphthous ulcers and in over 50% ocular inflammation occurs. Other features include arthritis, central nervous system involvement, skin lesions (e.g. erythema nodosum, folliculitis and acneiform lesions) and pathergy (abnormal response to tissue injury, e.g. skin ulceration following trauma or venepuncture). It commonly runs a relapsing and remitting course.

C Reactive arthritis

Oral aphthous ulceration is a feature of Crohn’s, but genital ulcers are not. Uveitis, which is suggested in the scenario, can be associated with a wide variety of conditions including Crohn’s, but is one of the commoner features of Behçet’s disease. Acne, whilst extremely common, is another feature supportive of Behçet’s. Overall, the constellation of findings in a Japanese patient, with no specific features of inflammatory bowel disease, make Behçet’s disease the best answer.

D Herpes simplex type I infection

Reactive arthritis usually follows a sexually transmitted infection (especially chlamydia) or gastroenteritis; arthritis is a key feature which is lacking here; otherwise, there may be urethritis (rather than discrete genital ulcers) and conjunctivitis. This tends to cause peri-oral rather than genital disease. Steroid treatment is likely to worsen it. Whilst it can be recurrent as in this scenario, there are many features here which it would not explain.

E Systemic lupus erythematosus

Treatment is largely symptomatic in mild cases, but systemic corticosteroids or immunosuppressants may be required by some.

questions.question: A 66-year-old retired labourer presents to his general practitioner (GP) complaining of an acutely swollen and red ankle. The attack started the night before with swelling and pain, and despite taking various analgesics, the pain intensified. He is a known hypertensive and suffers from congestive cardiac failure and osteoarthritis. He had previous similar episodes a few years ago. His current medications include bendroflumethiazide, lisinopril and amlodipine. On examination, the patient is apyrexial. There is a small, hard lump on his ear and he has a red, swollen and exquisitely painful right ankle, but he has full range of movement. Based on this patient’s history and clinical examination, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Septic arthritis

Septic arthritis should, however, always be considered in a mono-arthritis. Patients with crystal-induced arthritis may also present with fever and malaise, but he has no risk factors for septic arthritis such as recent penetrating injury or gonorrhoea, and the previous similar episodes suggest gout.

B Reactive arthritis

There is no infective precipitant – gastrointestinal or genitourinary. Reactive arthritis is usually an oligoarthritis (2–4 joints affected).

C Gout

He has had previous episodes or attacks before and has risk factors for gout, e.g. diuretic use, and has a tophus on clinical examination. Given that he has tophaceous gout, he should be started on allopurinol, when the acute attack has settled. Losartan could be started, in place of one of the other antihypertensives, the former having uricosuric action. Gout and pseudo-gout are conditions caused by the accumulation of crystals in the joint space resulting in pain, redness and swelling in the affected joints. Both conditions are more prevalent in males, gout more markedly so, and usually affect patients in the age range 30–60 years. Gout is caused by the accumulation of monosodium urate monohydrate crystals, whilst pseudo-gout is caused by the accumulation of calcium pyrophosphate crystals. In gout, the first metatarsophalangeal joint of the big toe is the site most commonly affected (the condition is known as ‘podagra’), with other common sites being the ankle, wrist and knee. The condition results from overproduction or reduced secretion of uric acid, with thiazide diuretics and foods that are rich in purines increasing the frequency of attacks.

D Pseudo-gout

Although it is difficult to reliably distinguish gout and pseudo-gout on clinical grounds, a tendency exists for gout symptoms to develop rapidly over a few hours, whereas the onset of symptoms in pseudo-gout tends to be more insidious and may occur over a period of several days. The joints affected by pseudo-gout usually include the knee, wrist and shoulder.

E Fracture of the ankle

A fracture without a history of trauma or injury and in the absence of osteoporosis is very unlikely.

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner with worsening shoulder pain and stiffness. Her symptoms are more pronounced in the morning and improve as the day continues. She has been trialling ibuprofen for the pain which has provided some relief. There is no history of headache or visual symptoms and she denies recent injury. Her past medical history includes hypertension, for which she takes amlodipine 10 mg daily. Her observations are recorded to be within normal limits. On auscultation, her chest sounds are clear and her heart sounds are normal. She has a soft and non-tender abdomen. There is bilateral shoulder and hip pain, with a reduced range of movement. Examination of her skin reveals no rashes or discolouration. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following features will most likely be present?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A C-reactive protein > 10 mg/L

This patient has polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR). PMR is an inflammatory condition that more commonly presents in women over the age of 60 years. It has similarities with the large vessel vasculitis, temporal or giant cell arteritis (GCA), and if visual symptoms are present, GCA should be considered, along with urgent referral to ophthalmology. PMR tends to have a rapid onset (< 2 months) and is characterised by proximal muscle pain and stiffness, which is worse in the morning and improves throughout the day. It should not be confused with polymyositis or diseases that cause proximal myopathy, which is associated with proximal muscle weakness.

B Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint stiffness

Antinuclear antibodies are markers used to assess for underlying autoimmune diseases. A positive ANA may or may not be seen in PMR and its presence is not specific to the disease, making it an unreliable diagnostic test. Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint stiffness is not a feature of PMR. PMR is predominantly characterised by proximal muscle pain and stiffness of the shoulder and hip girdles. Distal joint stiffness is not seen and is usually a sign of a different inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA). MCP joint stiffness is a common presenting feature of RA.

C Onset > 8 weeks

polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) typically has an acute onset of symptoms over a period of four weeks. A more delayed presentation suggests an alternative diagnosis such as degenerative arthritis.

D Positive antinuclear antibodies (ANA)

Laboratory investigations show an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein.

E Proximal muscle weakness

Proximal muscle weakness is not a symptom of PMR. Rather, proximal pain and stiffness are seen. Proximal muscle weakness suggests a different underlying disease such as polymyositis or myopathy.

questions.question: A 56-year-old woman presents with painful and itchy swellings on her knuckles. These are worse after exposure to sunlight and have been problematic for her for several weeks. She has a past medical history of type 2 diabetes, two pregnancies, one miscarriage and hypertension. She currently takes metformin and ramipril. Apart from the changes on her knuckles, she has not noticed any other changes. She denies any other rashes, joint stiffness or breathing problems. A photograph of her right hand is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Psoriasis

Lichen planus is a pruritic skin condition with polygon-shaped purple plaques on the lower back, wrists and ankles, as well as evidence of Wickham striae, white lines near sites of erosion. The location of this patient’s lesions does not match this diagnosis. Also, lichen planus is not worsened by sunlight. The mainstay of treatment for lichen planus is topical steroid treatment but can also include retinoids and UV light therapy.

B Dermatomyositis

The photograph shows Gottron’s papules on the patient’s right hand. This is a clinical sign pathognomonic for dermatomyositis. Dermatomyositis is a chronic, autoimmune condition which affects proximal muscles and skin primarily, but can also cause cardiac, pulmonary and rheumatological complications. Peak onset is at 50 years old with a slow but steady progression, causing diffuse weakness in proximal muscles, fatigue and myalgia. Distal muscles are spared. There can be systemic upset with fever, malaise and weight loss. A heliotrope rash is pathognomonic, and there can be also a photosensitive rash. Investigation is with autoantibodies: ANA, anti-Mi and anti-Jo antibodies can help establish diagnosis, but muscle biopsy may be necessary as a diagnostic investigation. Steroid treatment may be successful, but immunosuppressive therapy can be used as secondary treatment. Atopic dermatitis is a chronic skin condition characterised by itchy, dry and red skin, which comes out in flares of acutely inflamed, red and sometimes blistered skin. It affects particularly the flexural surfaces. It does not cause plaques as this patient has, except in very chronic cases. The association with sun exposure also makes this less likely.

C Atopic dermatitis

Psoriasis is chronic inflammatory dermatological condition defined by salmon-red rash with silvery plaques. It has several types. The most common pattern of presentation affects extensor areas over limbs with involvement of scalp, umbilicus, natal cleft and groin. The pattern of this patient’s rash is different in distribution and the appearance is not consistent with psoriasis.

D Lichen planus

Dermatitis herpetiformis is a persistent immunobullous disease linked to coeliac disease and characterised by pruritic clustering blisters symmetrically distributed on scalp, shoulders, buttocks, elbows and knees.

E Dermatitis herpetiformis

Management is with a gluten-free diet, and dapsone can be useful to reduce itch.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old banker was admitted with a 2-hour history of central crushing chest pain radiating down his left arm. He admits to abusing intravenous drugs in the past and is a life-long smoker. His past medical history includes hypertension and irritable bowel syndrome. On admission, a fast-track troponin level was raised. ECG demonstrated anterolateral ST segments elevated > 2 mm. He was treated for a myocardial infarction (MI) with intravenous thrombolysis followed by intravenous heparin infusion. ST segments returned to normal. Three days later in hospital this man developed a purpuric rash over his legs. On examination, there were normal heart sounds with no added murmurs. Chest examination revealed clinically a small left-sided pleural effusion. The abdominal examination was unremarkable. Neurological examination revealed weakness of his left arm: the patient felt this has been present for a while now since sustaining an injury playing football. ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm and anterolateral Q waves.

Blood results at this time show:

Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.6 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Urea15.0 mmol/L2.5 - 6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)179 μmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)150 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)87 mm/h1 - 20 mm/h
ANAPositive
ANCANegative
Haemoglobin (Hb)100 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)11.4 × 10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 × 10⁹/L
Neutrophils8.0 × 10⁹/L1.5 - 7.0 × 10⁹/L
Eosinophils0.09 × 10⁹/L0.04 - 0.4 × 10⁹/L

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Microscopic polyangiitis

In this scenario, the test for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) is negative which rules out microscopic polyangiitis.

B Polyarteritis nodosa

The American College of Rheumatology states that patients must have three of the following to have a diagnosis of polyarteritis nodosa (PAN): weight loss >5 kg, livedo reticularis, testicular pain/tenderness, myalgia, mono/polyneuropathy, diastolic BP >90 mmHg, elevated urea/creatinine, hepatitis B virus. This man clearly has a systemic vasculitis given a history of cardiac, gastrointestinal and renal involvement. The recent neurological involvement clinches the diagnosis of PAN.

C Streptokinase-induced vasculitis

A vasculitis secondary to streptokinase occurs mainly in those who have received previous streptokinase therapy and does not explain the other manifestations. It is an immune-complex phenomenon and antistreptokinase antibodies can be measured. Renal impairment can occur.

D Systemic lupus erythematosus

Patients with SLE tend to present with other skin manifestations and low platelets.

E Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)

GPA affects the respiratory tract more commonly. There is no mention of ear, nose and throat symptoms in this

questions.question:
A 45-year-old Asian woman presents with 3-month history of difficulty climbing stairs. She also described non-specific pain all over her joints, the lower legs and upper arms. She has been seeing her general practitioner for her symptoms, and several analgesics have been tried, but her symptoms are not improving. She is on insulin for diabetes and bendroflumethiazide for mild hypertension. On examination there is slight tenderness on the upper arms and the lower legs but not at multiple trigger points. Respiratory and cardiovascular examinations are normal.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)110 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.6 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)200 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)135 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.8 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)102 μmol/L50–120 mol/l
Corrected calcium (Ca²⁺)2.08 mmol/L2.20–2.60 mmol/L
Phosphate(PO₄³⁻)0.69 mmol/L0.70–1.40 mmol/L
Creatinine kinase (CK)200 U/l23–175 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)150 mmol/L30–130 IU/L
X-ray of the lower legs shows coarsened trabecular bone, no fracture.

What diagnosis will you consider the most likely in her case? 43
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Fibromyalgia

The patient has an abnormal bone profile and does not have tenderness at multiple trigger points on examination. Fibromyalgia is a diagnosis of exclusion.

B Polymyositis

The patient’s main symptoms are generalised bony pain, she has an abnormal bone profile and her CK is only mildly elevated. Osteomalacia can cause a proximal myopathy.

C Osteoarthritis

The patient’s bone profile and her clinical features of generalised bone pain are suggestive of osteomalacia and she is too young for generalised osteoarthritis.

D Osteoporosis

Osteoporosis is associated with normal bone profile.

E Osteomalacia

The patient has slightly low calcium, low phosphate and high ALP. Osteomalacia results from inadequate mineralisation of bone due to deficiency in vitamin D. Inadequate sunlight exposure (particularly in some Asian women who wear protective long clothing), in combination with dietary deficiency is often seen as a cause. Other causes of osteomalacia are chronic kidney disease, renal osteodystrophy, malabsorption and renal tubular defects etc. Osteomalacia may result in symptoms such as skeletal pain and tenderness, proximal muscle weakness and spontaneous fractures. X-ray of long bone is often normal but may show defective mineralisation, with the characteristic ‘Looser’s zone’ (pseudofractures). Biochemistry shows low calcium, phosphate, vitamin D levels and raised ALP.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman presents to the Rheumatology Clinic with widespread musculoskeletal pain, fatigue and difficulty sleeping, which have been ongoing for over a year. She describes her pain as 'aching all over' and notes that it often worsens with stress. She has been evaluated by multiple specialists, and extensive testing has ruled out other conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and hypothyroidism. She has tried over-the-counter analgesics with minimal relief. Physical examination reveals multiple tender points, but no signs of joint inflammation or swelling.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)140 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)6.5 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)240 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)2.1 mIU/l0.4–4.0 mIU/l
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)10 mm/hour< 20 mm/hour

Given this patient's diagnosis of fibromyalgia, what is the best way to manage her symptoms?
options: Start high-dose NSAIDs on a daily basis
Refer to Rheumatology for immune-modulating therapy
Prescribe high-dose opioids for pain relief
Recommend a structured exercise programme combined with cognitive behavioural therapy
Initiate corticosteroid therapy to reduce inflammation
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Start high-dose NSAIDs on a daily basis

NSAIDs have limited efficacy in fibromyalgia, as the pain is not primarily due to inflammation. They may provide some relief for mild musculoskeletal discomfort but should not be used as a primary treatment.

B Refer to Rheumatology for immune-modulating therapy

Immune-modulating therapies are unnecessary, as fibromyalgia is not an autoimmune condition. Management should focus on lifestyle interventions, non-pharmacological therapies and, if needed, medications that target pain perception rather than immune function.

C Prescribe high-dose opioids for pain relief

Opioids are not recommended for managing fibromyalgia due to their limited efficacy in chronic pain syndromes and a high risk of dependency. Non-pharmacological strategies, such as exercise and CBT, have shown greater long-term benefits for symptom control in fibromyalgia patients.

D Recommend a structured exercise programme combined with cognitive behavioural therapy

Exercise, particularly aerobic activity, has been shown to improve physical function and decrease pain in fibromyalgia. Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is also effective in helping patients manage the psychological aspects of chronic pain. Together, these non-pharmacological therapies form the basis of fibromyalgia management, as per guidelines from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence.

E Initiate corticosteroid therapy to reduce inflammation

Corticosteroids are not indicated in fibromyalgia, as it is a non-inflammatory condition. This therapy would be ineffective and expose the patient to unnecessary side-effects.

questions.question: A 57-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with complaints of pain and yellowish discharge from a wound in the left foot for the past ten days. He says that it started after sustaining a puncture wound to his left foot two weeks ago. The patient says that he was not walking barefoot and had his shoes on when he sustained the injury. He did not seek medical attention at that point in time. He has no other co-morbidities. On examination, his blood pressure is 110/60 mmHg, heart rate 102 bpm and temperature 37.9°C. Local examination reveals warmth, redness and tenderness over the right foot and a purulent discharge from the wound over the left first metatarsophalangeal joint. An X-ray of the patient's foot is taken: Which of the following is the most likely pathogen implicated in the infection from which this patient is suffering?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Coagulase-negative staphylococci

Coagulase-negative staphylococci are common pathogens isolated in implant-related infection.

B Mixed anaerobic infection

Mixed anaerobic infections are common in patients who have had polytrauma and have a large amount of devitalised tissue, thereby enhancing the growth of anaerobic organisms.

C Pseudomonas aeruginosa

This patient’s signs and symptoms and radiological examination are suggestive of acute osteomyelitis. In a patient who is a non-diabetic who has sustained a puncture wound, studies have shown that P. aeruginosa is the most common cause of acute osteomyelitis. P. aeruginosa can also cause infection after piercing of the ear cartilage.

D Staphylococcus aureus

Image Source: James Heilman, MD, CC BY 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons In a diabetic, the most common cause of acute osteomyelitis after a puncture wound is S. aureus. This patient is not diabetic. Overall, in patients with no history of a puncture wound, the most common cause of acute osteomyelitis is S. aureus.

E Streptococcus pyogenes

S. pyogenes is a common cause of skin and soft tissue infection but only infrequently causes acute

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman complains of pain in the right ankle that she has experienced for the past 3 weeks. Two or three days later, she notices that the ankle is also swollen. A week later, this is followed by pain and swelling in both knees. Her general practitioner (GP) started diclofenac 50 mg three times daily, which alleviated the pain to some extent. She further remembers having loose bowel movements for a few days about 10 days prior to the onset of joint symptoms. She informs you that she sometimes develops loose bowel movements after eating a takeaway. Medications other than non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) include paracetamol, which she takes for intermittent backache, and salbutamol and beclomethasone inhalers, for bronchial asthma.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)137 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)4.8 × 10⁹/L4.0–11.0 × 10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)188 × 10⁹/L150–400 × 10⁹/L
Neutrophils2.1 × 10⁹/L2.5–7.58 × 10⁹/L
Lymphocytes1.8 × 10⁹/L1.5–3.5 × 10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)18 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour
C-reactive protein (CRP)21 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)28 IU/L10–40 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)101 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)15 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Glucose5.5 mmol/L3.5–5.5 mmol/L

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Ankylosing spondylitis (AS)

There is a clear infective precipitant and although she has back pain, we are not given any features of inflammatory back pain to suggest spondyloarthritis.

B Reactive arthritis

This lady has an oligoarthritis following a likely gastrointestinal infection. Asymmetrical arthritis, predominantly involving large joints in lower extremities, is suggestive of the seronegative spondyloarthropathy type of arthritis. Reactive arthritis is most likely with the preceding history of diarrhoea. Her inflammatory markers are modestly elevated. Reactive arthritis is aseptic inflammatory arthritis, usually triggered by chlamydial urethritis or cervicitis or enteric infection with Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter or Yersinia in a genetically susceptible individual. HLA B27 is the major currently known genetic risk factor. The arthritis usually resolves in 3 months but can recur or become chronic.

C Septic arthritis

She has an oligoarthritis following a diarrhoeal illness. Septic arthritis may be a polyarthritis in 10% of cases, but usually patients are far more sick (with signs of systemic sepsis) with red, hot swollen joints and can barely move these affected joints. Blood results are not overtly helpful for differentiating causes here, but one might expect a higher CRP and white cell count with septic arthritis. NB: Gonococcal septic arthritides are usually associated with a pustular skin rash and red, linear areas of tenosynovitis.

D Gout

This lady has a spreading oligoarthritis following a diarrheal episode. Gout is usually a sudden-onset, exquisitely painful arthritis. This young female patient does not have any risk factors for gout either.

E Still's disease

Still's disease is associated with fevers, a rash and small joint polyarthritis over a more prolonged period than is seen .

questions.question:
A 20-year-old man presents with a 1-month history of intermittent fever accompanied by chest pain, which is worse on lying down. He has recently also noticed pain in the joints of his hands and feet. He is febrile, with a temperature of 39 °C. His pulse is 98/min and his blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. The positive findings on examination are enlarged anterior cervical lymph nodes, pericardial rub, mild hepatomegaly and synovitis of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and wrist joints.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)105 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)20 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)540 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)110 mm/hour1–20 mm/hour
C-reactive protein (CRP)246 mg/L<10 mg/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)69 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)246 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Ferritin4567 µg/L20–250 µg/L
Chest X-ray (CXR)Cardiomegaly—
2-D echocardiogramPericardial effusion—
MSU and blood cultureNegative—
ANA, RF, ANCA, anti-CCPAll negative—
CT abdomenHepatosplenomegaly—

Which of the following is most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

A very high fever, raised CRP, organomegaly and negative ANA make SLE very unlikely. SLE is associated with a normal CRP and an elevated ESR. The presenting symptoms in SLE can be very variable due to the condition having multi-system effects ranging from indolent to fulminant, but the classic presentation is of the triad of arthralgia, fever and malar rash in a woman of child-bearing age.

B Mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD)

A very high fever, raised CRP, organomegaly and negative ANA make MCTD very unlikely. MCTD is a term used to describe a condition that features overlap of autoimmune connective tissue disorders with certain laboratory findings to match. It is recognised to consist of core features including arthritis/arthralgia, acrosclerosis, myositis, oesophageal dysmotility, pulmonary hypertension, lung fibrosis, raised anti-U1-RNP antibodies and antibodies against U1-70 kd small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (snRNP).

C Undifferentiated connective tissue disease (UCTD)
